The Provincial Sexual and Reproductive Health Program developed two main strategies for reducing abortion-related maternal mortality [4].

Care has been provided since 2007 to women seeking abortion, consisting of the risk and harm reduction model developed by "Iniciativas
evidence.location: Introduction and Materials and methods, offsets 2200-3300
evidence.reason: Matía et al. (2016) describe and evaluate the public health policies implemented by the Province of Buenos Aires Ministry of Health through the Provincial Sexual and Reproductive Health Program (PSSR), combining primary-care risk and harm reduction counseling (started in 2007 and modeled on 'Iniciativas Sanitarias' in Uruguay) with primary-care legal termination of pregnancy (LTP) services (started in 2012) and manual vacuum aspiration training (started in 2014). The paper reports descriptive 2010–2015 service provision counts across four municipalities and provincial maternal and abortion-related mortality trends from 2010 to 2014. Although the title and text refer to 'replicating the Uruguayan risk and harm reduction model' and discuss transferability to primary care, this refers to adopting and transferring a clinical service delivery model into a new public policy setting rather than conducting an empirical test of a specific prior published mortality claim. The shipped original study, Briozzo et al. (2006) (10.1016/j.ijgo.2006.07.013), is never cited in the text or reference list (only Briozzo & Faúndes, 2008 [Ref. 6] is cited in the Discussion regarding health professionals' willingness to provide legal abortion services), and the authors explicitly note that provincial maternal mortality reductions cannot be credited to the evaluated primary health units alone. Under the Codebook, transferring a clinical/policy service model without empirically retesting a prior published research finding is not_a_replication.

expected_before.outcome_quote: we show that, consistent with our previous finding, global deletion of Irs1 significantly extends lifespan in female mice. In addition, an augmented and completed study demonstrates lifespan extension in male Irs1 null mice.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, we replicate and validate our previous finding [12] that global deletion of Irs1 induces a robust lifespan extension in female mice. Therefore, we now clearly show that, in addition to the GH deficient dwarf mice [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] , [21] , [22] , female Irs1 −/− mice also show a highly consistent and repeatable lifespan extension across distinct studies. In common with the Ames dwarf mouse lifespan studies [17] , [18] , the two separate lifespan studies in female Irs1 −/− mice were undertaken in the same vivarium, albeit at different times. We suggest that replication of survival data, such as ours and those of the GH dwarfs [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] , [21] , [22] , will significantly help increase confidence in exactly what genetically modified mice are valid models of retarded aging [13] , [14] . In turn, this confidence should focus time and resources on those interventions that will ultimately help us to understand what mechanisms underlie healthy aging in humans. It should be noted that one additional limitation in mouse longevity studies is that they are generally performed in a single genetic background, e.g. C57BL/6. We suggest that it will be highly informative for future studies to examine longevity in mice, such as Irs1 nulls, across different genetic backgrounds. We also show that, in contrast to our earlier study [12] , a completed and augmented lifespan study in male mice indicates that median lifespan is extended in male Irs1 −/− mice by ∼16%. This new finding suggests that the lack of any effect was probably due to an incomplete and slightly underpowered earlier study in males [12] , with larger sample sizes undoubtedly helping to detect relatively subtle changes between genotypes [23] .
evidence.reason: The original study [12] reported lifespan extension in female Irs1-/- mice but no lifespan effect in male Irs1-/- mice. This paper re-tests female lifespan in an independent cohort—confirming the female finding—and reports a completed and augmented male lifespan study that found significant lifespan extension in males, explicitly framed as 'in contrast to our earlier study [12]'. Under the codebook rules, finding an effect where the original found none is a disagreement with the original result, and when the authors explicitly mark one tested result as differing from the original ('in contrast to our earlier study [12]') while another agrees, the aggregated outcome is 'mixed'.

evidence.quote:
Richard Easterlin claims it has not. In a seminal paper entitled 'Does economic
      growth improve the human lot?' he argues that happiness remained at the same level in
      the US between 1946 and 1974, in spite of a doubling in income per head over that period
      (Easterlin 1974). In later papers Easterlin showed that this pattern persisted in the US and
      that it also appears in other countries (Easterlin 1995, 2004). This position has come to be
      known as the 'Easterlin paradox' and is generally taken as a fact.
               We challenged this view in a recent article in this journal, entitled Wealth and
      Happiness Revisited: Growing National Income Does Go with Greater Happiness
      (Hagerty & Veenhoven 2003). In the paper we presented the trend data on average
      happiness in 21 nations for the years 1972-1994 and showed that happiness had increased
      in most of these nations, including the USA. Consequently we found a positive
      correlation with economic growth.
               Richard Easterlin elegantly disputed these findings in a paper: Feeding the
      Illusion of Growth and Happiness: A Reply to Hagerty and Veenhoven, published in this
      journal (Easterlin 2005).
evidence.location: Section 1 Introduction, page 1, lines 22-36 (reference on page 18, lines 733-735)
evidence.reason: Under the codebook rule on replication chains, when a finding has already been re-tested by others, the target is the study closest to this paper in the chain that it actually re-tests, not the chain's original source. Easterlin (1974) is cited as the seminal origin of the Easterlin paradox, which was extended in Easterlin (1995, 2003/2004), challenged by Hagerty and Veenhoven (2003), and then re-asserted and empirically defended by Easterlin (2005) regarding separate US survey series, Western Europe trends, and developing nations including Japan. This paper ('A reply to Easterlin') directly replies to and re-tests Easterlin (2005) across those three empirical domains using expanded 1946-2004 survey series.

The central finding of the present analysis is that overeducated workers have worse

career prospects than correctly allocated workers. This is in clear contrast to the

results put forward by Sicherman (1991). Note, however, that we were able to

replicate the US results with our German data when using Sicherman’s approach.

Therefore, the key to understanding the puzzling pattern of results is to be found in a

discussion of the validity of the indicators chosen to indicate upward career mobility,

and the quality of specification in Sicherman’s model.
evidence.reason: In Section 4.1 (Table 2, Columns II-III), the authors closely replicate Sicherman's (1991) occupational upward-mobility specification using German GSOEP data and obtain the same positive, statistically significant effect for overeducation. However, their central argument is that Sicherman's specification and indicator are flawed: controlling for starting occupational rank ('base'/ceiling effects, Table 2, Column V) renders the overeducation effect insignificant, and replacing occupational rank moves with a valid indicator of upward career mobility (relative wage growth controlling for base wages, Section 4.2, Tables 3-4) reverses the effect. Under the codebook rules, obtaining the original effect with the original approach while demonstrating as the paper's main message that the original method/specification does not validly test the hypothesis is coded as 'statistically successful but flawed'. The shipped coding ('failed') relied only on the abstract's summary of the wage-growth specification.

expected_before.outcome_quote: We did not replicate prior findings with regard to learning outcomes: learning was neither facilitated nor compromised when seeing the instructor's face.

evidence.quote:
The main aim of this study was to attempt to conceptually replicate the findings by Van Gog et al. (2014). That is, we first hypothesized that participants in the Face Visible with Gaze Guidance condition would allocate a substantial amount of attention to the instructor's face, meaning that they would pay significantly less attention to the task than students in the No Face Visible condition (H1). In line with this hypothesis, we indeed found that participants who saw the instructor's face paid less attention to the task area than participants who did not see the face.
Second, we expected participants in the Face Visible with Gaze Guidance condition to outperform participants in the No Face Visible condition on the test tasks eat least after having seen the example twice (H2a,b). However, we did not replicate this finding: seeing the instructor's face had neither beneficial nor detrimental effects on learning in the present study.
evidence.reason: The authors explicitly define replicating the findings of Van Gog et al. (2014) in terms of two main tested hypotheses: attention allocation (H1) and learning performance (H2a,b). In the Discussion, they report that the attention-allocation finding was replicated (H1), whereas the beneficial effect on learning outcomes was not replicated (H2a,b), and they also note an opposite direction for the change in looking time across viewings (Q1, line 70). Because one tested finding of the original study was confirmed while another explicitly failed to replicate, the outcome is mixed under the codebook.

evidence.quote:
In 2012, our research team initiated an effort to replicate Tschudin’s follow-up experiments. The goal
was to replicate as much of Tschudin’s methodology as could be determined from the summary in his 2006
paper given that the training protocol used to teach the dolphins, the various aspects of the task, and the timeline
it took to prepare the dolphins for the task, were not provided (Table 3). To fill any gaps in Tschudin’s

Tomasello (1999), including limiting the number of FBTs presented so as to control for the effect of experience.
evidence.location: A Case Study - Attempted Replication, p. 10, lines 558-563 (see also Discussion, p. 13, line 654; References, p. 22, lines 1043-1044)
evidence.reason: Prior adjudication and state files (adjudications/12db194db4781556.json, argon/12db194db4781556.state.json) were checked and do not exist; prior expert result (fields_12db194db4781556_000.result.json), independent validation (source_validation_0003.result.json), Crossref metadata (10.1017/s0962728600023563), blind coding, and full primary text were reviewed. Answering the scope objection: Hill et al. (2018) conducted a single 2012 case study and did not independently re-test two separate target papers. Under the codebook replication-chain rule, the target is the closest study actually re-tested: Tschudin (2006), which re-tested the same four dolphins from Tschudin (2001) (plus a fifth naive dolphin) with added controls. The Case Study section explicitly states that the 2012 effort was initiated to replicate Tschudin's follow-up experiments from his 2006 summary, the Discussion explicitly calls the experiment an attempted replication of Tschudin's study (2006), and the protocol implements the 2006 controls (visible displacement trials and modified 'dud' true belief trials, neither of which was conducted in the 2001 pilot, Table 3) plus target-pole tapping. References to Call and Tomasello (1999) and Tschudin (2001) (e.g., planning 12 displacement and 4 FBT trials) supply unstated procedural details to fill gaps in the 2006 report rather than establishing a separate empirical re-test of 2001. Replacing the shipped 2001 entry with Tschudin (2006) and attaching target_index 1 reconciles row 349 with blind target 1 without creating a false missing pair.

The shipped quote ('To summarize, for this experiment we found results that were in the same direction as the original study and statistically significant where predicted.') only summarizes the first two experiments (lines 299 and 390). In the third experiment (AML patient samples, replicating Figure 5), the authors explicitly qualify their conclusion because the planned confirmatory comparison on IDH1-mutant samples using total ion chromatograms (TIC) was not statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.063) and showed nonsignificant meta-analytic pooling (p = 0.114) with significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q p = 0.031). proofs.quote:
We replicate and expand a recent study by Simonovits, Guess,

and Nagler (2019) to explore if its conclusion – a pronounced and uniform conservative

bias – has stood.

We demonstrate that, averaged across states, policy change closely tracked a
pronounced increase in preferences for higher minimum wages, but the size of
policy bias remained relatively stable. However, this national pattern hides
an increasingly polarized policy landscape: in many states, insuﬃcient respon-
siveness led to an increasing deviation between preferences and policies, while
in other states policy changes – larger than preference changes – closed initial
policy bias.

It
shows that the median bias hovered between $2 and $3 throughout our study period: it
grew from $2.2 in 2014 to $3.1 in 2016, then decreased to $2.5 in 2019, and grew again
to $2.8 in 2021. Meanwhile, policy bias in minimum wage laws also reﬂects an increasing
polarization in the US. The range of biases grew steadily from $2.7 in 2013 to $3.3 in
2016, $4.9 in 2019 and $6.1 in 2021. No state had a liberal bias in 2014, and the smallest
conservative bias was in Oregon at $1. By 2021, ten states had less conservative bias

than that, and three states (California, Washington, and DC) had a liberal policy bias.

evidence.quote: Excluding inconsistent reporters had a modest average effect on past 30-day alcohol use (mean relative change: −8.9%), but substantial heterogeneity was observed. In eight datasets, prevalence decreased by at least 15%, reaching −29.4% in Ghana. Effects were, on average, larger in younger students and males. Excluding inconsistent reporters occasionally strengthened or reversed age- and sex-related patterns.
evidence.reason: The shipped 'successful' outcome is an error based on a sentence stating that the prevalence of inconsistent reporting in LMICs corroborates prior findings on inconsistent reporting in high-income countries, not that Ma et al.'s (2018) substantive prevalence findings held. In fact, re-analyzing the data after excluding inconsistent reporters substantially altered prevalence estimates (up to -29.4%), occasionally reversed age- and sex-related patterns, and reordered or eliminated alcohol acquisition sources, establishing 'robustness challenges' (while computational reproducibility of the unadjusted numbers cannot be determined from the abstract alone).

evidence.quote: Based on a data-adjusted replication of a study in 57 LMICs, this work assessed the effect of inconsistent reporting on prevalence estimates. Methods To standardize the operationalization of inconsistent reporting, I examined the 37 datasets that contained the exact same set of items. Inconsistencies were identified based on logical contradictions. Prevalence estimates of past 30-day alcohol use and sources of alcohol acquisition were computed using unadjusted data (i.e., including all reporters) and adjusted data (i.e., excluding inconsistent reporters).
evidence.reason: Although the author uses the term 'data-adjusted replication', the study re-analyzes 37 of the original 57 LMIC survey datasets by comparing estimates from the unadjusted data (including all reporters) with adjusted data (excluding inconsistent reporters). Under the codebook, re-analyzing the original study's data under an alternative inclusion rule is a reproduction, not a replication.

This study presents a replication and extension of the original study (Spadini et al.
2018) by examining a broader range of projects on GitHub, the most representative
platform of the PR review model. The results for RQ1 confirm that reviewers primar-

evidence.location: Primary raw context chars[80352,80715); original-specific Methods/Results/Discussion independently inspected
evidence.reason: Under the codebook, confirming one tested effect is a single comparison rather than an overall replication verdict, and when a paper reports some findings as agreeing with the original study while explicitly marking others as differing from the original, the outcome is mixed. Here, the authors confirm Spadini et al. (2018) on reviewers primarily focusing on production code in mixed PRs (RQ1 Scenario A) and reviewing production code before test code (RQ3, 74.33%), but explicitly contrast their findings with the original study on overall attention balance and Scenario B odds ratios (RQ1) as well as test review discussion topics (RQ2, where GitHub reviewers focus much more on superficial code improvements and less on defect detection and comprehension than in Gerrit). Parent primary-source confirmation: Primary Discussion confirms the original production-first review finding, while Introduction/Results explicitly contrast GitHub versus original Gerrit review balance and test-discussion topics. The newly studied GHA temporal effect is an extension, not itself a failed original finding; the platform-specific original comparisons nevertheless contain both agreement and disagreement, supporting mixed.

expected_before.outcome_quote: In general, this multisite experiment supports the psychological relevance of nature imagery for stress recovery, while highlighting important nuances in physiological responses.

evidence.quote:
Taken together, the present multisite study partially confirmed the
original findings by Ulrich et al. (1991), demonstrating that viewing
nature imagery promotes psychophysiological recovery. However, the
results for physiological responses highlight the nuanced ways in which
exposure to natural and urban environments may influence psychophysiological stress recovery.
evidence.reason: The authors explicitly state an overall verdict that their study 'partially confirmed' and 'partially replicate[d]' the original findings of Ulrich et al. (1991). While self-reported psychological recovery (positive affect and anger/aggression) and initial parasympathetic recovery in the forest condition replicated the original results, recovery from fear and sympathetic physiological recovery (SCR and PEP) did not replicate greater recovery in natural conditions, and the stream condition failed to replicate physiological recovery. Under the codebook rules, both the explicit partial-confirmation verdict and the combination of replicated and non-replicated effects require coding the outcome as 'mixed' rather than 'successful'.

expected_before.outcome_quote: demographic and experimental findings on Lucid track well with US national benchmarks, with the exception of experimental treatments that aim to dispel the 'death panel' rumor.

evidence.rationale: The shipped mixed outcome is not supported for the Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz (2012) experimental findings. The abstract explicitly says that the same analyses are replicated; Figure 2's introductory text compares Lucid, MTurk and original experimental estimates; Experiments 1–4 report shared findings rather than merely citing a method. Most decisively, Experiment 3 states the risk-acceptance finding and that it replicated in both MTurk and Lucid, and Note 10 explicitly identifies Berinsky et al. (2012) as the report of that earlier replication. These are new-sample retests of the earlier replication's reported empirical finding, permissible under the closest-actually-retested chain rule. Calling the paper a methodological template or naming its older source does not negate this relationship. The current source reports the same qualitative risky-choice conclusions across all three samples, agreement for welfare wording, and similar experimental estimates for free trade. For free trade, the sentence about the combined frame names original and MTurk only; it does not state a Lucid disagreement, while the authors explicitly judge the studies similar. No overall verdict specifically on the 2012 target supersedes these comparisons; applying outcome rule 2 to the shared experimental findings supports successful. The discussion's sole substantively different experiment is explicitly Berinsky (2017), and the main text says that experiment has no prior MTurk replication. Its healthcare-rumor divergence must not be inherited by the 2012 target. The outcome correction is conditional on parent resolution of the original-row dependency: the evidence supports retaining the earlier-replication target, whereas unconditional not_applicable/removal is not supported by the prior template-only rationale. Parent owns any original-field change, closest-chain reconciliation and duplicate removal across sibling targets; this result assigns only outcome. No claim of report equivalence or distinctness rests on DOI/year alone.

contrary_evidence.quote:
Berinsky et al. (2012) demonstrated the validity of
MTurk by replicating classic experiments originally conducted on probability samples; we follow their lead and do

the same on Lucid. As an empirical matter, our Lucid replications recover very similar treatment effect estimates to the
original studies.
contrary_evidence.response: The introduction describes following Berinsky et al.'s validation approach and names older original studies. This supports a template role but does not exclude its concurrent empirical role. The abstract, direct three-sample comparisons, and Note 10 establish actual retesting of at least its Kam–Simas replication finding. The first-round argument treated these roles as mutually exclusive without sufficient evidence.

proofs.quote:
Our point of departure is the 2012 study by Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz that compares
Amazon’s Mechanical Turk to US national probability samples in terms of respondent characteristics and treatment
effect estimates. We replicate these same analyses using a large sample of survey responses on the Lucid platform.

In the Welfare,
Asian Disease, Kam and Simas, Hiscox and Berinsky facets found in Figure 2, we present standardized treatment
effect estimates, where we have scaled the outcome variables for Lucid and MTurk by the mean and standard deviation of the original experiments. The Berinsky facet does
not include an MTurk estimate since it has not been previously replicated on an MTurk sample.

This experiment behaves on Lucid
much as it does on MTurk and the GSS – a large increase in
support for redistribution when the question is phrased as
assistance or caring for the poor rather than as “welfare.”

Across all three samples (the original experiment was
conducted in a classroom setting among undergraduates),
the treatment has average effects in the same direction,
with subjects in the mortality (loss) frame far more likely
to choose the probabilistic (risky) outcome, though the
magnitudes of the effects do differ substantially by

The Expert frame increases support

10. Berinsky et al. (2012) analyze the original and their replication using a probit model, but we use ordinary least
squares (OLS). While some analysts prefer to use nonlinear models like logit or probit when the dependent variable
is binary, in an experiment, OLS (without adjustment) is
unbiased for the ATE (or, as in this case, the CATEs). See
Gerber and Green (2012: ch. 2) for a textbook proof. The
substantive conclusions do not change in any way if we use
probit regression.

We conclude our set of five experiments with a note of caution. We attempted to replicate Berinsky’s 2017 experiment
on belief in rumors surrounding the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), specifically the false rumor that the ACA would
create “death panels” that would make end-of-life decisions
for patients without their consent. In the original experiment (conducted in 2010 on a sample provided by Survey
Sampling International (SSI)), a large portion of the sample
believed the rumor, and corrections delivered by
Republicans, Democrats, and Nonpartisan groups were all
effective in correcting false beliefs.

Among our five experiments, we have one instance of
the Lucid sample producing substantively different
results compared to the original study. In no way do we
think our results contradict or overturn those reported by
Berinsky (2017).

evidence.quote: To resolve this debate and enable an accurate estimate of effect size, we replicated the key paradigms in this research stream using well-powered, pre-registered studies with participants drawn from the broader population. The first experiment investigated the immediate emotional rewards of prosocial (vs. personal) spending by providing participants the opportunity to spend a small monetary windfall on edible treats for themselves or an unknown sick child at a local children’s hospital (see Aknin et al., 2013, Study 3). Afterward, participants reported their current well-being. The second experiment used a recollection procedure (as in Aknin et al., 2013, Studies 2a-b) in which participants were randomly assigned to reflect upon a previous purchase made for themselves or others before reporting their well-being.

As a first step in assessing the replicability of motor
compatibility effects, we conducted a pre-registered, multi-lab
replication of the ACE. We used an adapted version of the
original ACE paradigm (Glenberg & Kaschak, 2002) that was
used in Borreggine and Kaschak (2006). The choice of this
particular version of the ACE paradigm was somewhat arbitrary. We had no strong a priori reasons to expect that one
paradigm or the other would produce a stronger or more reliable ACE. Ultimately, we chose the Borreggine and Kaschak
(2006) paradigm over the original Glenberg and Kaschak
(2002) paradigm in part because we sensed that this paradigm
would be slightly easier to execute across a large group of
labs.
evidence.reason: Under the codebook rule on replication chains, when a finding has already been re-tested or adapted by others, the target is the study closest to this paper in the chain that it actually re-tests rather than the chain's original source. evidence.quote:
A recent study by Riccucci et al. (2016) indicates that symbolic gender representation is an important quality for
citizen–state interactions. Increasing the representation of female officials positively affected the willingness to
co-produce in a recycling initiative. The results suggest that women were more willing to co-produce when encountering higher shares of female officials. These findings promise considerable benefits for public organizations, as
symbolic representation may lead to better services as well as cost savings (Riccucci & Van Ryzin, 2017). However,
Van Ryzin et al. (2017) conducted a recent replication with a different policy context that could not confirm the
findings. Symbolic representation did not unfold in the context of emergency preparation.
Consequently, Van Ryzin et al. (2017) proposed additional replication studies “as an opportunity to further
develop and test the underlying theory of symbolic representation to more deeply probe its mechanisms and contingencies” (p. 1376). Following this notion, the present study provides a wide replication (Walker et al., 2019) of the
original research by Riccucci et al. (2016).

evidence.quote:
In summary, the main similarities observed between the original group and the present group were on the level of (un)knowledge about statistical terms and the use of statistical techniques, given that they seem to know the same statistical terms and techniques, and the statistical techniques they said they do not know and do not use are approximately the same. These findings suggest that both academic groups receive similar statistical and methodological training in their countries. evidence.quote:
A recent genome-wide association study by the International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium (IMSGC) reported
association of 17 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 14 loci with multiple sclerosis (MS). Only two loci, HLA-DRA
and IL2RA, reached genome-wide significance (Po5E08). In our study, we determined whether we could replicate the results
of the IMSGC and whether more SNPs are genome-wide significantly associated with MS. We assessed the association between
the 17 IMSGC SNPs and MS in three cohorts (total number of subjects 3981, among these 1853 cases). We performed a
meta-analysis of the results of our study, the original IMSGC results and the results of a recent replication study performed in
the Australian population. Of the 17 IMSGC SNPs, five SNPs showed genome-wide significant association with MS: HLA-DRA
(P¼8E124), IL7R (P¼6E09), IL2RA (P¼1E11), CD58 (P¼4E09) and CLEC16A (P¼3E12).Therefore, genome-wide
significance has now been shown for SNPs in different non-HLA MS risk genes.
evidence.reason: Hoppenbrouwers et al. (2009) tested all 17 top candidate SNPs reported in the initial IMSGC (2007, 10.1056/nejmoa073493) genome-wide association study across three independent multiple sclerosis cohorts and a combined analysis of 11,376 individuals. While 5 SNPs reached genome-wide significance (HLA-DRA, IL7R, IL2RA, CD58, and CLEC16A) and EVI5 was independently replicated, the remaining tested IMSGC SNPs did not reach genome-wide significance, and for three IMSGC loci (PDE4B, DBC1, and ANKRD15) the authors explicitly report on p. 677 that 'our results suggest that the previously reported association in the initial IMSGC screen was a false positive association.' Because some tested original loci from IMSGC (2007) replicated and others failed as false positives, the paper-level outcome is mixed.

expected_before.outcome_quote: the results show effective equity constraints when explaining debt levels, as observed in the Californian sample

evidence.quote: After having removed outliers, the results show effective equity constraints when explaining debt levels, as observed in the Californian sample with respect to the overall amount of debt. The results also indicate an agency explanation of debt: both the decision to borrow from financial institutions, and the overall amount of (financial) debt are positively affected by the presence of a potential agency gap between board and management. In the Californian sample, the results on this were mixed. Borrowing constraints were almost never discovered, similar to the conclusions reached by Jegers and Verschueren. However, slightly reducing the sample by removing outliers makes borrowing constraints apparent.
evidence.reason: The study re-tests three capital structure theories from Jegers and Verschueren (2006) without stating an overall replication verdict, and its comparisons show partial agreement (equity constraints after outlier removal and full-sample borrowing constraints) alongside divergence (clear agency effects where the original was mixed, and borrowing constraints becoming apparent once outliers are removed).

evidence.quote:
Concerning the replication part of our project, our results support the view that CT is
underpinned by reasoning, as assessed by figural reasoning, and spatial abilities, as
assessed by visualization. However, in contrast to the original study, we also found
a significant association between CT and mental arithmetic.
evidence.reason: For the resolved original study (Román-González et al., 2017), the replication tested the contributions of figural reasoning, visualization, and mental arithmetic to computational thinking (CT), as well as gender differences. While the authors replicated the positive associations and unique regression contributions of figural reasoning and visualization (and higher male CTt scores, though not fully explained by cognitive skills), they explicitly mark the mental arithmetic result as diverging from the original null finding ('However, in contrast to the original study, we also found a significant association between CT and mental arithmetic' and 'Our observation of a small positive association between mental arithmetic and CT does not replicate previous findings by Román-González et al. (2017)'). Under the codebook, confirming part of the tested findings while explicitly contrasting another tested finding as not replicating yields a 'mixed' outcome.

evidence.rationale: A bibliographic correction to the explicitly cited journal target is supported by the current paper’s specific aim, model provenance, original sample/effect and full printed reference. The codebook instructs following that citation and distinguishing a meeting abstract from the published article. This narrower correction is supported without certifying conference/journal empirical equivalence. It supersedes the earlier conclusion that equivalence must be resolved before even proposing citation correction. The new supplements fully document the journal sample and analysis but supply no conference crosswalk; thus the shipped conference citation cannot be confirmed as the report actually named by current. The correction must be integrated as the cited journal pair, not as proof that the conference is the same or a different empirical study.

contrary_evidence.claim: Shared consortium, investigators, broad older-brain conclusion and similar sample magnitudes allow a preliminary/final relationship; lack of a crosswalk does not establish distinctness.
The conference Results and Conclusion conflict; neither should be silently repaired to make it match the journal.

We are able to reproduce the
AJR reversal in terms of the territorial entities that constitute present-day
countries. But we show that with respect to the people who live in countries and
their descendants, there was no reversal. AJR (2002) demonstrated their reversal
on the basis of two main indicators of development in 1500: the rate of
urbanization, and population density. We find that in the large fraction of AJR’s

evidence.quote:
As the only attempt to replicate
7
in the field so far, this study successfully reproduced that study’s main finding: The email response rate was significantly higher in the “money” condition than in the “no money” condition. Nevertheless, this study also expanded our understanding of civic honesty in theoretical and empirical ways.
First, our study contributed to the field of civic honesty research by revealing the significant limitations of using a single, potentially culturally biased index to measure the level of civic honesty in a society. We found that relying solely on the email response rate as a measure of civic honesty could underestimate its actual level in China.
evidence.reason: The authors explicitly state that their field experiment successfully reproduced the original study's main finding on the original metric (a significantly higher email response rate in the money vs. no-money condition, alongside a similarly low overall email response rate in China). However, the central substantive message of the paper—reflected in its title, abstract, employee and national surveys, and wallet-recovery extensions—is a construct-validity critique of the original study's reliance on email response rate as the sole measure of civic honesty. The authors demonstrate that email response is a culturally biased indicator that conflates individualistic proactive outreach with civic honesty and fails to capture collectivistic safekeeping norms, thereby underestimating civic honesty in China and producing opposite treatment effects when actual wallet and contents recovery are measured. Under the codebook, obtaining the original effect while arguing as the paper's main message that the original measure does not validly test the construct takes the special verdict 'statistically successful but flawed'.

expected_before.outcome_quote: the original pattern of findings was largely upheld: Older children were more likely to verbalize, and their memory spans improved.

evidence.quote: Work by Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966) indicated a change in the spontaneous production of overt verbalization behaviors when comparing young children (age 5) to older children (age 10). Despite the critical role that this evidence of a change in verbalization behaviors plays in modern theories of cognitive development and working memory, there has only been one other published near-replication of this work (Keeney, Cannizzo, & Flavell, 1967). This Registered Replication Report relied upon 17 labs who contributed their results to a larger and more comprehensive sample of children. We assessed memory performance and the presence or absence of verbalization behaviors of young children at different ages, and determined that the original pattern of findings was largely upheld: older children were more likely to verbalize, and their memory spans improved. We confirmed that 5- and 6-year-old children who verbalized recalled more than children who did not verbalize. However, unlike Flavell et al., substantial proportions of our 5- and 6-year-old samples overtly verbalized at least sometimes during the picture memory task. evidence.quote:
For 1980 Piketty reported that he averaged the 1983 figure from Wolff [1994] with the
1989 Federal Reserve figure from Kennickell [2009]. Had he done that, the number would be
67.7, but he reported 67.2 (which is the 1989 figure unaveraged). For 1990 Piketty’s spreadsheet
noted that he averaged three figures from “Kennickell 2001 Table 4” for the years 1992, 1995,
and 1998 [TS10.1DetailsUS]. But actually he used Kennickell [2009: Table 4, 35] [Piketty
2014b: 57]. The averaging procedure should have given him 67.8, but he reported 68.7,
probably a typo.
evidence.reason: Because the study type is a reproduction, the outcome must be coded on the two reproduction axes. On computation, following Piketty's stated averaging and adjustment procedures in his spreadsheets fails to recover several reported values due to calculation and spreadsheet errors ('computational issues'). On robustness, alternative and consistent constructions of the same underlying historical sources (such as applying the 1.2 household multiplier consistently to the 1870 top-10% estimate or avoiding arbitrary interpolations and constant 36-point markups) materially qualify or reverse the claimed historical trends ('robustness challenges').

evidence.quote: By means of a laboratory experiment, Rubin and Sheremeta (Manag Sci 62(4):985–999, 2016 ), study a bonus-version of the gift-exchange game, including two treatment variations. First they vary whether the effort provided by the agent directly translates into output for the principal, or whether it is distorted by a shock. Second, for the condition with a shock they vary whether the shock is observed by the principal, or not. The authors’ main findings are that (1) the introduction of an unobservable shock significantly reduces welfare; and (2) informing the principal about the size of the shock does not restore gift-exchange. In a replication study we largely reproduce finding (1), but we fail to confirm finding (2).

expected_before.outcome_quote: thereby replicating 3 out of 4 effects.

evidence.quote:
The present study is a pre-registered replication of a study by Specker et al. (2018) that tests the
hypothesis that brightness of colors is associated with positivity. Our results showed an implicit association
between brightness and positivity in both Study 1 and Study 2, however, an explicit association between
brightness and positivity was only found in Study 2, thereby replicating 3 out of 4 effects. To investigate
these effects in more detail, we present a meta-analysis of both the original and the replication study.
This indicated a large effect 1.31 [1.12, 1.51]. In addition, we used meta-analysis to assess potential
moderators of the effect, in particular stimulus type (chromatic vs. achromatic) and measure type (implicit
vs. explicit). This indicated that the effect is stronger when measured implicitly than when measured
explicitly and that the effect is stronger when achromatic stimuli are used. In sum, we take these findings
to indicate that there is a strong and replicable association between brightness and positivity.
evidence.location: Abstract, p. 1, lines 14-22 (and Introduction, p. 2, lines 80-85; Study 1 Method & Discussion, pp. 2-3, lines 115-117, 161-164; Study 2 Discussion, p. 5, lines 280-283; Figure 3, p. 6, lines 302-322)
evidence.reason: Both shipped row 936 and blind target 0 coded 'mixed' based on the phrase 'replicating 3 out of 4 effects', but a full reading of the primary source shows that all three empirical findings actually reported in the original Specker et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.actpsy.2018.04.007) paper replicated. Specifically, the authors explicitly state that in the original Specker et al. (2018) paper, Study 1 (chromatic patches) included only an implicit IAT measure, whereas Study 2 (achromatic patches) included both an implicit IAT measure and an explicit rating task ('In the original study only Study 2 included an explicit measure, for our replication we also included this measure in Study 1', Introduction, p. 2, lines 80-83; 'Our method, materials and procedure was identical to Study 1 of Specker et al. (2018), thus we used an IAT the only difference being that we included an explicit rating task', Study 1 Method, lines 115-117; corroborated by Figure 3, lines 302-322, which plots only Study 1 Original Implicit, Study 2 Original Implicit, and Study 2 Original Explicit). Every original study result replicated with large effects: original Study 1's implicit chromatic association replicated ('Study 1 replicated the findings of Study 1 of Specker et al. (2018) meaning that both studies found a large effect for the implicit association of brightness and positivity', lines 161-164, dz = 1.73), and original Study 2's implicit (dz = 4.07) and explicit (dz = 3.06) achromatic associations both replicated ('Study 2 replicated the findings of Study 2 of Specker et al. (2018) meaning that both studies found a large effect for the implicit and explicit association of brightness and positivity', lines 280-283). Although the authors remark that 'Study 1 did not show an explicit effect for the association between brightness and positivity that should theoretically have been there, we therefore interpret this as a failure to replicate' (lines 164-167), that fourth test was a newly added extension condition in Study 1 testing a theoretical expectation rather than a comparison against an existing Study 1 finding of Specker et al. (2018). Under Codebook Step 3 (Rule 1: overall verdict governs; Rule 2a: a comparison requires an actual finding reported by the original study; and under 'mixed': 'A count of how many measures replicated is not by itself such a mark') and FIELD_REVIEW_INSTRUCTIONS.md ('Main-message hierarchy in the codebook governs outcomes: use the authors' overall verdict where supplied... New extension/control outcomes do not automatically change replication outcomes'), all original comparisons succeeded and the authors' overall conclusion ('In sum, we take these findings to indicate that there is a strong and replicable association between brightness and positivity', Abstract lines 21-22; General Discussion lines 392-393, 441-443) establishes 'successful'.

Bayes Factor analyses found that in each case the evidence for a variability benefit was ambiguous. This means that null effects are not established but also indicates that this type of training paradigm is not sufficiently sensitive to detect variability benefits. We suggest that, if it does exist, such a benefit in phonetic training is likely very small.
evidence.reason: The outcome is 'failed' rather than 'uninformative' or 'mixed'. First, the authors explicitly demonstrate that their study was not underpowered or defective as a test of the original claim: in Discussion (line 164, and simulations in line 73 / footnote 0), they emphasize that their sample of 166 participants (versus 6 per experiment in the originals) had a 99% chance of detecting the original HV benefit (OR = 1.37) if it were truly there, and conclude that 'if an effect exists, it is likely much smaller than the effect reported by Logan et al. (1991) and Lively et al. (1993)'. Second, they explicitly treat the original multi-talker advantage as unconfirmed ('the findings of this replication are different from those of the original study', 'the current replication study finds no substantial evidence for a HV benefit', line 166; 'multi-talker training might not confer a specific advantage', line 168; 'Across two different measures, our study found no evidence of such effect in a sample of 166 participants', line 178). This
study explores the nature of this individual variation through three speech sound categorization
tasks: one where both lexical and coarticulatory biases are present simultaneously for the /s-ʃ/

and coarticulatory effects (r= -0.19), weaker but consistent with Lai et al. (2022). There was no
evidence for a trade-off across tasks; a joint Bayesian model that estimated individual-level
correlations across tasks showed that lexical and coarticulatory effects were not credibly related.

consistent across tasks. Overall, the findings suggest that while trade-off patterns can be replicated
within specific tasks, they are not robust across tasks, indicating possible task-specific effects or
contrast-specific perceptual strategies.

evidence.location: Introduction, p. 5 (see also Abstract, p. 1, Sections II-III, pp. 6-11, and Conclusion Section IV, p. 12)
evidence.reason: Across two distinct data streams—(1) reanalysis of Malmendier and Lee's (2011) shared data (Section II, where the cross section shows 60% vs. 37% overbidding by 'new' title wording, mean auction prices exceeding mean low BINs for only 22/88 products, and 150 item mismatches, while Cashflow 101 lacks auction titles so the primary wording test cannot be applied directly, alongside a corrected shipping-fee programming error in fn. 19) and (2) a new 552-auction eBay movie-DVD dataset (Section III)—Schneider statistically reproduces significant overbidding (23% of DVD auctions, with no decline across experience in fn. 20, though mean auction price is 18% below mean low BIN and overbidding is 35% vs. 15% by wording). evidence.quote:
In conclusion, a narrow replication produced a coefficient 48% larger than the coefficient
reported by OS although it should have been identical, and although the results are qualitatively
unchanged, I find the difference disconcerting. However, a slightly broader replication,
including a measure of the economy’s health, indicated a considerably larger economic impact
of piracy that is inconsistent with their conclusion.
evidence.reason: On the computation axis, re-running the original specifications on the publicly available datasets produced substantive numerical discrepancies across the analyses (including a 48% larger coefficient on what should have been an identical monthly regression in Table 3, an 8.8% vs. 12% summer piracy drop in Table 1, an opposite-signed genre coefficient in Table 5, and unrecovered data claims in Section 5), establishing 'computational issues'. On the robustness axis, reasonable alternative specifications and variable constructions on the same underlying datasets (separating summer dummies in Table 1, removing unallocated sales to compare East/West market share ratios in Table 2, controlling for unemployment in Table 3, and correcting the genre piracy intensity denominator in Table 5) overturn the original conclusions, establishing 'robustness challenges'.

One study, however, is considered particularly convincing evidence for dual-process
accounts (Sweldens et al., 2014). In this study, Rydell, McConnell, Mackie, and Strain
(2006) showed a selective influence of briefly presented USs on implicit attitudes. In this
experiment, the CS was a picture of a character named Bob, which was preceded by a briefly
presented prime and followed by explicit, behavioral information about Bob. Prime and
explicit information had opposite valence. The key finding of the study is that explicit
attitudes were affected by behavioral information, whereas implicit attitudes reflected the
valence of the briefly presented prime. Rydell et al. (2006) conclude that their participants
held opposite implicit and explicit attitudes at the same time reflecting on the two types of
information received. A prime-recognition check at the end of the study confirmed that the

evidence.quote: In the absence of the beacon, participants in group Ambient tended to make path choices in the test that were adjacent to the location of the path that led away from the central chamber during the training phase. This pattern does not conform to that anticipated by Tolman et al., which assumes path choices in the test that were based on the shortest route to the goal location experienced during training. However, in group Light-Light, a close replication of the arrangement in the study of Tolman et al., path choices tended toward the paths leading to the goal/light. This pattern is what would be expected if, contrary to their arguments, the light acted as a beacon indicating proximity to the goal.
evidence.reason: Addressing the parent scope objection: in the close replication of Tolman et al.'s original experimental arrangement with a goal-proximal light (group Light-Light), the authors reproduced the original goal-directed path-choice effect, but their central thesis—demonstrated by the disappearance of short-cutting when the beacon confound is removed (group Ambient) or shifted (group Light-Shifted) and by the lack of correlation with map drawings—is that Tolman et al.'s method is confounded by beacon guidance and does not validly test cognitive-map short-cutting. Under the codebook, recovering the original effect under the original procedure while showing as the paper's main message that the original method is not a valid test of the theoretical claim codes as 'statistically successful but flawed', rather than 'failed' (which ignores that the original light-present design reproduced the empirical effect) or 'mixed' (which treats the deconfounding control comparison as partial support for the original claim).

evidence.quote: We reproduced a past case study on land-use change induced land degradation in a Mediterranean ecosystem ("Vegetation Dynamics 1.0" [42]), which was conducted before the opening of the Landsat archive, and well before the remigration of European data holdings into the main data archive, thus inevitably being limited by data scarcity. Now, for the first time, the complete cross-calibrated data record over Europe was available and allowed to replicate this study with a state-of-the-art, data-driven, phenology-adaptive methodology based on the peak of season metric ("Vegetation Dynamics 2.0"). Following our findings, we conclude that trends derived from a Vegetation Dynamics 1.0 methodology are systematically prone to uncertainty due to a volatile timing of statically selected images relative to the spatially and inter-annually variable phenological cycle-sometimes close to peak vegetation cover, while other times close to minimal vegetation cover. This is especially critical if:
evidence.location: Section 5 Conclusions, p. 19 (chunk 59, chars 53073-54065); see also Section 4.1, pp. 13-15 (chunks 42-47)
evidence.reason: Frantz et al. (2022) revisit Hostert, Röder, & Hill (2003) [42] on an expanded spatial and temporal Landsat archive covering all semi-natural areas of Crete for 1984-2006 (2,816 images, omitting pre-1984 MSS data). In Phase 1 (Vegetation Dynamics 1.0), they reconstruct the original static image-selection method (14 cloud-free dates near peak vegetation) and explicitly report thematic reproducibility of Hostert et al. [42] and Sonnenschein et al. [49]: net change is negative (50% decreasing vs. 26% increasing), resembling Hostert et al.'s >40% decline in central Crete (Psiloritis). However, in Phase 2 (Vegetation Dynamics 2.0), using the full archive and phenology-adaptive peak-of-season (VPS) metrics alongside woody/herbaceous decomposition and breakpoint analysis, the net trend reverses to positive vegetation gain (18% decreasing vs. 50% increasing), and interactive expert validation confirms only 32.9% of VD 1.0 trends vs. 98.7% of VD 2.0 trends. Because the study thematically recovers the original result when applying the original static-selection method, but its central message is that the VD 1.0 methodology is systematically flawed and produces spurious negative trends due to volatile phenological timing, the codebook category 'statistically successful but flawed' applies.

Contrary to the original paper’s assertions, we find no evidence that analysts exhibit a consistent positive

evidence.quote: When excluding fixed effects and trend variables, I found that states with WSPs had about 20 percent fewer unemployed low‐income females. The inclusion of fixed effects and trend variables, which Kim and Berry reported using in their model, caused the WSP variable to become about 0 percent and insignificant. The results of the synthetic control methods provided additional evidence that questions the validity of the original findings. Conclusions Kim and Berry's research seemingly contains significant flaws, including incorrect results.
evidence.reason: With the record type resolved to reproduction, outcome is coded on the two reproduction axes. Re-running the original difference-in-differences specification with the fixed effects and trend variables that Kim and Berry reported using yielded a ~0% insignificant effect rather than the reported ~18% reduction (which only appeared when excluding those controls), establishing 'computational issues'. Supplementary difference-in-differences and synthetic control analyses also challenged the validity of the original causal finding, establishing 'robustness challenges'.

evidence.quote: We replicate Andreoni (Quarterly Journal of Economics 110: 1–21, 1995 )’s finding that agents behave more selfishly when taking from a public account than when giving to a public good. Based on a neutral language setting we add new insights into motivations to give or take in a linear public good setting: we find that Andreoni’s result is partly driven by the complete elimination of giving options in the taking frame. However, a pure extension of the action space into the taking domain also leads to a significant increase in selfish behavior.
evidence.reason: The authors state an explicit overall verdict that they replicate Andreoni's (1995) finding, and their additional treatments decomposing the mechanism still find a significant increase in selfish behavior in the taking domain rather than a conflicting or failed result.

al.’s (2022) results. The first area of difference is seen in applicant rank. Luo et al. found that student

evidence.quote: Although goalkeepers were jumping more often towards the left or right and staying less often in the center, they had statistically similar chances of stopping the goal for both decisions. Additionally, there were more kicks to the left and right compared to the center. Thus, we conclude that jumping is not a sub-optimal action for goalkeepers and high frequency of jumping is not indicative of action ‘bias’, which suggests competent decisions by these professional goalkeepers during penalty kicks.
evidence.reason: Although goalkeepers jumped left or right more often, the key empirical premise of the original action-bias claim—that staying in the center is optimal—failed to replicate because goalkeepers had statistically similar save rates for both actions. The authors' explicit overall verdict (and title) is that there is no action bias and jumping is not suboptimal, supporting 'failed' rather than 'statistically successful but flawed'.

evidence.quote: The replication of their preferred specification delivers almost identical estimation results. The present contribution proposes a two-step estimation approach that takes into account the variation induced by the estimation of the fixed effects in the first step and leads to consistent estimates of the standard errors. evidence.quote: The replication of their preferred specification delivers almost identical estimation results. However, AAT do not consider that the dependent variable of the supply function is a vector of estimated parameters, the fixed effects of the demand-side gravity model. The present contribution proposes a two-step estimation approach that takes into account the variation induced by the estimation of the fixed effects in the first step and leads to consistent estimates of the standard errors. Moreover, the estimates of the supply curve parameters turn out as highly sensitive to the specification of the demand-side gravity model, limiting the applicability of AAT’s approach.
evidence.reason: Despite using the word 'replication' in the title and abstract, the study re-estimates the original authors' preferred specification (obtaining almost identical results) and conducts econometric extensions and specification sensitivity checks (a two-step standard-error adjustment and alternative demand-side gravity specifications) rather than testing the finding in a new sample. Under the codebook, re-analyzing the original model and testing specification robustness is a reproduction.

expected_before.outcome_quote: We do not find a link between ADHD and EO, although we do find a positive link between ADHD and the risk-taking subdimension of EO. Hyperactivity symptoms are positively related to EO, which is mainly driven by the subdimensions proactiveness and risk-taking. We do not find a link between attention-deficit symptoms and EO, though there is a negative link between attention-deficit and proactiveness.

evidence.rationale: The newly recovered published journal contains the two selected aggregate-EO findings: a positive hyperactivity/impulsivity association and a nonsignificant joint-model inattention association. The current report explicitly states those original findings and reports agreeing results. Its overall-ADHD and EO-subdimension differences are extensions, not contrasts with an original tested claim. Under codebook rule2 this supports successful rather than shipped mixed. Journal Study2 support is marginal, not p<.05, and its bivariate inattention correlation must not be confused with the conditional structural estimate. Version provenance remains explicit; no universal result-equivalence rule was adopted.

contrary_evidence.claim: The replication explicitly used the 2018 proceedings version; it did not retrospectively target the journal version. This provenance remains true. The new source establishes selected-finding correspondence, not identity of every estimate, specification, or result across versions.

Journal Study 2 positive hyperactivity–EO evidence is marginal (p=.076), its 95% bootstrap CI crosses zero, and hyperactivity/impulsivity composite reliability is .397. Study 1 is more strongly supported; do not describe both original studies as p<.05. Authors' supported/marginally supported reading and the same positive claim do not turn this replication's agreeing result into mixed.

Study 1 journal bivariate inattention–EO correlation is positive r=.161, p<.05 (Table 1), whereas the joint structural-model estimate is null/negative −.081, p=.417. The selected finding corresponds to the fitted models with both symptom dimensions, not an assertion of zero association under every specification. Study 2 bivariate r=.176 is unstarred; its joint-model inattention coefficient is also nonsignificant.

EO definitions and estimators differ: Yu treats firm-level EO as a second-order reflective construct using maximum likelihood SEM; Wismans uses individual-level aggregate EO with OLS and reflective/formative PLS-SEM. Yu Study 1 uses ASRS-18 with three items dropped (one inattention, two hyperactivity/impulsivity); Study 2 uses ASRS-6 and drops an innovativeness item. Wismans uses ASRS-6, different controls and French SME owners. These are conceptual-replication differences explicitly relevant to scope, not evidence that the selected claims changed direction.

Wismans' overall ADHD null, positive ADHD–risk-taking and EO-subdimension findings are extensions. Yu discusses the three EO dimensions theoretically and speculatively, but does not provide separate symptom→EO-dimension tests as selected findings; it explicitly says its data do not allow completely unpacking the scales. Wismans' negative attention-deficit–proactiveness and absent hyperactivity–innovativeness relations do not contradict a separately estimated journal result. Firm-performance and mediation claims in the journal were not selected by Wismans and need not all be replicated for this outcome.

proofs.quote:
Studying the sub-dimensions of ADHD using OLS, hyperactivity is posi-
tively related to total EO (β = .10, p < .01), and attention-deficit is not asso-
ciated  with  total  EO.  Using  PLS-SEM,  we  found  similar  results  for  these 
relationships (hyperactivity: β = .11, p < .01). In terms of the EO dimensions, 
hyperactivity is not related to innovativeness but is related to both proactive-
ness (β = .10, p < .01) and risk-taking (β = .09, p < .05). Attention-deficit is 
not related to innovativeness and risk-taking but is related to proactiveness 
(β = −.11, p < .01).

Looking at the subdimensions of ADHD, the results of our analyses are 
mostly in line with the findings of Yu et al. (2018). Similar to Yu et al., we 
found a positive association between hyperactivity and EO. This effect seems 
to be driven by a positive relationship of hyperactivity with the subdimen-
sions proactiveness and risk-taking and not by a relationship with innovative-
ness. We do not find a link between attention-deficit and total EO. However, 
we do find a negative link between attention-deficit and proactiveness.

Although  we  do  not  find  an  overall  relationship  between  ADHD  and 
EO, we provide insight into the underlying links between the two constructs. 
Furthermore, we are able to replicate the positive relationship found by Yu et 
al. (2018) between hyperactivity and EO using another data set.

reliability expected from lower item counts.

(2017) and strongly supported their conclusion, attributing weaker correlations in the exploratory strict reconstruction to lower reliability from fewer items. expected_before.outcome_quote: Computational: While trying to reproduce the results from the study using the original paper’s data and analysis code, we found many different issues. These issues included claims that did not match the provided evidence, statistical results that could be unreliable, group comparisons based on values beyond a scale’s possible range, inflated effect sizes due to a statistical artifact, and numbers we could not reproduce with the original data and code.

evidence.quote:
According to the results of the new model we ran, the expected difference in discernment score between someone with the lowest news sharing habit
    score (score of 1) and someone with the highest news sharing habit score (score of 7) is 0.036 (on average, all else equal). In other words, the strongest
    possible habitual sharers would be expected to make a discerning decision 3.6% less often than the weakest possible habitual sharers. This effect size
    feels at odds with descriptions in the paper, such as “As predicted, and replicating Study 1, strongly habitual participants continued to share with limited
    sensitivity to the veracity of headlines.”
    In sum, it appears that the analytical approach used throughout the paper to assess discernment may have caused inflated effect sizes because of the
    fact that stronger habitual sharers tended to share a medium amount of the headlines while weaker habitual sharers tended to share very few of the
    headlines. That said, the general finding that higher habitual sharers had worse discernment held even when calculating discernment differently. The
    effect was just weaker.
evidence.location: Study and Results in Detail > The way discernment was calculated may have inflated the difference between strong and weak habitual sharers, p. 21, lines 893-901
evidence.reason: Shipped 'not checked' is wrong because the authors explicitly re-analyzed the original Study 2 data under alternative variable constructions and estimators (both a full-sample linear regression using participant-level proportion of discerning decisions on pp. 19-21 and four preregistered subgroup analyses in the Appendix on pp. 36-39). Blind 'cannot_be_determined' is also wrong because it relied only on the underpowered Appendix subgroup analyses that the reviewers discounted as uninformative, overlooking the main-text full-sample re-analysis (lines 835-901, 1061-1065). In that alternative specification removing the logistic model's baseline-rate artifact, the standardized effect of news sharing habit on discernment dropped from -0.41 (p < 0.001) to -0.07 (p = 0.035)—only a 3.6% difference across the entire 1-7 scale—which the reviewers explicitly judge to be much weaker, at odds with the original paper's descriptions, and unclear as to practical meaningfulness, satisfying 'robustness challenges' (at least one reasonable alternative analysis materially weakens or substantively qualifies the original finding).

evidence.rationale: The complete current Transparency Trail and complete newly supplied SPSS/AMOS text, including all seven AMOS pages, plus the entire SEM image were read. The original-data re-analysis actually changes item inclusion and scoring: removal of item 19, reversing Intrinsic rather than Extrinsic items, and subtracting from 6 rather than sign-flipping; these are source-motivated alternative variable constructions, not mere computational reruns. Under the revised grouping, posted I WTP mean 4.0074 exceeds E 3.4620; the explicit E-then-I test ordering explains the negative reported t (-5.115). That comparison preserves the original substantive group ordering. For the other explicitly targeted claim, the original states that I/E was the only significant WTP predictor and neither age nor gender was significant. The posted revised SEM reports sex standardized .404, p .004, alongside age .194, p .160 and the focal predictor .894, p .004. Sex becoming significant materially qualifies that original-specific exclusivity claim; it is part of the quoted target claim, not an unrelated exploratory result. This independently supports robustness challenges, even though the group difference survives. Neither the numerical mismatch nor the report's unsuccessful precise-reproduction verdict supplies this robustness judgment. The new outputs settle the previously missing group means/order and age/sex paths. A narrower construct-mapping ambiguity remains: the diagram and output label the latent predictor Extrinsic, whereas the report describes E/I parcels after reversing Intrinsic items and quotes an original I/E claim. The mixed parcel loadings do not establish that this is the original intrinsic construct with the same orientation. I therefore do not relabel the predictor, flip its direction, infer a substantive reversal, or claim that .894 confirms the original intrinsic association. The significant sex comparison does not require resolving that latent sign: it qualifies the explicitly targeted only-significant-predictor result in the posted revised model. Shared W1/W2 loading labels across constructs and W3 across the focal structural path and EI_p3 loading, standardized indicator loadings of plus/minus 1, and poor reported fit (CFI .000; RMSEA .288) substantially limit the model's scientific interpretation. The result supports a qualified challenge in this attempted re-analysis, not proof of a well-fitting alternative model or proof that the original substantive effect is false. These limitations neither establish an author-uninformative verdict nor justify ignoring the observed original-specific comparison. The review is complete for the assigned robustness field only.

contrary_evidence.claim: Shipped not checked and original numerical success criteria could restrict the evidence to computational reproducibility.
contrary_evidence.response: The criteria are computational, but the documented, source-motivated changes to variables were actually analysed on original data. The independent axis must consider their substantive results.

contrary_evidence.claim: Prior reviewed_unknown depended on missing revised group means/order and age/gender paths.
contrary_evidence.response: The authenticated posted outputs now supply both. Their exact t and standardized focal path match the report's rounded values. The old unavailability statement no longer applies.

contrary_evidence.claim: The negative t implies reversal of the I/E group result.
contrary_evidence.response: Explicit SPSS E-I order and I mean above E show that the group finding persists; no statistic was recomputed.

contrary_evidence.claim: The larger positive focal SEM path proves robust, or its Extrinsic label proves substantive reversal.
contrary_evidence.response: Neither follows without an unambiguous construct/orientation mapping. The challenge rests instead on the newly significant sex path against the original's explicitly stated exclusivity claim.

contrary_evidence.claim: Fresh blind coding proposes robustness challenges; poor SEM fit or suspicious loadings could instead require cannot_be_determined.
contrary_evidence.response: I independently agree with challenges on the narrow exclusivity comparison. The output limitations are real and prevent a confident directional focal-construct verdict; they are retained, rather than recast as an author verdict or a reason to erase the source-motivated variable-construction test and its reported qualifying result.

missing_evidence_or_policy_choice.evidence_limit: Latent Extrinsic versus original I/E orientation is not fully resolved by the text/figure. The exact implemented measurement constraints are also not scientifically justified in the report. These limit interpretation of the focal SEM path and generalization of this challenge; the posted sex result already qualifies the expressly targeted exclusivity claim without choosing a latent sign. No remaining missing group means or age/sex paths, and no access failure, is asserted.

evidence.reason: In the supplied abstract-only source, Haun et al. (2011) found that both Dutch-speaking (egocentric) and Hai||om-speaking (geocentric) children had difficulty using their language-incongruent reference frame. In Experiment 1 (the replication), this difficulty held for Tseltal-speaking children (matching Hai||om-speaking children) but not for English-speaking children, which the authors explicitly describe as 'discrepancies between present English- and previous Dutch-speaking children.' Under the codebook, 'statistically successful but flawed' requires both that the original empirical effect was obtained and that the main message argues the method does not validly test the hypothesis. Neither requirement holds in the abstract: first, the original cross-group effect was only partially recovered in Experiment 1 rather than obtained in full (the shipped 'successful' quote comes from full text absent from the source); second, task order and instruction comprehension are proposed cautiously ('may explain') and tested via follow-up extension experiments (Experiments 2-5) to reconcile conflicting literature under a competing causal account ('suggest that task constraints, rather than language, determine which system is easier to use'). Because Experiment 1 reports one agreeing comparison and one explicit discrepancy with the original study, the outcome is 'mixed'.

evidence.quote:
First, in
Experiment 1
, despite the use of a larger sample and an experimental procedure devoid of the limitations present in the original experiment, we were not able to replicate Bargh et al's
[1]
automatic effect of priming on walking speed. This led us to assume that crucial factors in this paradigm had remained unidentified.
Experiment 2
was aimed at exploring such factors.
Second, in Experiment 2 we were indeed able to obtain the priming effect on walking speed for both subjective and objective timings. Crucially however, this was only possible by manipulating experimenters' expectations in such a way that they would expect primed participants to walk slower. Our results, however, cannot be explained solely in terms of a pure self-fulfilling prophecy effect
[14]
, as the primed participants did not walk faster when tested by an experimenter who believed they would walk faster. Therefore it seems that the primes alone are not sufficient and must be in line with environmental cues such as the experimenters' behavior in order to elicit the effect on walking speed.
evidence.reason: Both experiments re-test Bargh et al. (1996, Studies 2a and 2b) on new samples. Shipped ('failed') quotes only Experiment 1's null result and ignores Experiment 2, where the walking-speed priming effect was replicated on both subjective and objective infrared timings when experimenters expected slower walking. Addressing the parent scope objection regarding 'statistically successful but flawed' versus 'mixed': (1) the baseline double-blind replication in Experiment 1 failed statistically rather than succeeding through a methodological flaw; (2) across the Abstract and full Discussion, the authors explicitly reject a pure methodological-artifact or self-fulfilling-prophecy explanation (objective slowing occurred only when age primes and slow expectations combined, not under fast expectations, and stopwatch error only affected fast-condition subjective timings), concluding in the Abstract that 'unconscious behavioral priming is real, while real, involves mechanisms different from those typically assumed to cause the effect' and framing the conditional Experiment 2 effect in the Discussion as context-sensitive priming; and (3) while the Discussion notes above-chance 4-AFC prime recognition and awareness of slowing (leaving complete unawareness 'unclear' and urging methodological caution), the authors suggest awareness may have impaired rather than produced priming expression. Because the paper reports a failed baseline replication in Experiment 1 alongside a conditional context-dependent replication in Experiment 2 and partial awareness contrasts, the aggregated outcome is 'mixed'.

A logistic regression was conducted because the original analysis, a 2x2 between subjects ANOVA, could not accurately analyze data with so few respondents. Confirmatory analysis did not replicate the original finding that participants from the hot list donated more in the to-go condition than in the to-date condition, while participants from the cold list also donated more in the to-go condition than the to-date condition. Specifically, while approach priming had no effect and the self-esteem x perceived partner criticism interaction failed on most dependent variables, the confirmatory regression on behavioral support provision in the note (B = .301, SE = .145, beta = .357, p = .042, with a marginal three-way interaction p = .054) and exploratory separated support-seeking analyses supported the original hypothesis for low vs. high self-esteem under partner criticism. Under the codebook, this explicit partial replication verdict is 'mixed' (blind_right).

evidence.quote: We did not find evidence that participants offered fewer chips to angry recipients than to happy recipients in low-consequences situations, as van Dijk et al. (2008) did; hence, we did not replicate the key effect of their Experiment 3. In addition, we did not find a difference in the number of chips offered to angry vs. happy recipients in high-consequences situations. However the absence of this effect in the high-consequences condition resembles the original study, as well as the lower variances of offers made in the high-consequences condition and higher variances of offers made in the low-consequences condition do. Furthermore, we did find a number of effects that resemble other effects that were evident in the original study.
evidence.location: 9fed70371eeb17ff.source_view.json, chunks 381-382 (Primary Project Report: https://osf.io/download/2idfu/, Summary of Replication Attempt)
evidence.reason: The shipped coding ('failed') relied on a synthetic summary string ('Coded as not replicated: Replicate = 0...') rather than the primary report text. In the primary replication report for van Dijk et al. (2008, JPSP 94(4), 600-614; target_index 36), the Analysis Plan specifies confirmatory tests for multiple predictions from Experiment 3: chips offered in the low-consequences condition (the key effect), manipulation checks, likelihood of acceptance, importance of rejection, recipient's perceived limit, and participants' own emotions. In the Summary of Replication Attempt, the authors report that they did not replicate the key simple effect on chips offered in the low-consequences condition (nor the emotion main effect/interaction on likelihood of acceptance or emotion effect on perceived limit), but explicitly contrast this with several other tested predictions from the original study that did replicate (including the main effect of consequences of rejection on chips offered, the absence of an emotion difference in the high-consequences condition and the variance pattern across conditions, the main effect of consequences of rejection on importance of rejection, the effects of recipient emotion on participants' own emotions, and the main effect of consequences of rejection on likelihood of acceptance). Under the codebook, calling one test the 'key effect' does not override a stated contrast in the conclusion when both replicated and non-replicated substantive predictions from the original are reported without a holistic verdict dismissing the others; therefore, 'mixed' (blind_right) is correct.
