expected_before.outcome_quote: High-demand participants recalled an average of 54.3% {SD = 12.2) of the words, substantially fewer words than the 69.8% (SD = 11.4) recalled by low-demand participants, f(36) = 4.06, p < .001, ci = 1.35, replicating the Schmeichel (2007) finding.

evidence.quote: Schmeichel (2007) reported that performing an initial task before completing a working memory span task can lower span scores and suggested that the effect was due to depleted cognitive resources. We showed that the detrimental effect of prior tasks depends on a match between the stimuli used in the span task and the preceding task. A task requiring participants to ignore words reduced performance on a subsequent word-based verbal span task but not on an arrow-based spatial span task. Ignoring arrows had the opposite pattern of effects: reducing performance on the spatial span task but not on the word-based span task. Finally, we showed that antisaccade, a nonverbal task that taxes domain-general processes implicated in working memory, did not influence subsequent performance of either a verbal or a spatial span task. Together these results suggest that while span is sensitive to prior tasks, that sensitivity does not stem from depleted resources.
evidence.reason: The authors obtain the prior-task decrement on working memory span when task stimuli match, but their central message is that this effect is an artifact of stimulus overlap rather than valid support for Schmeichel's (2007) cognitive resource-depletion hypothesis.

evidence.quote: Discussion We performed a close replication of Experiment 2 by Mitchell and colleagues (2008) and partially replicated their results. We find a similar main effect of same versus different trials, but no main effect of training condition (AX/BX versus CX). Instead, our data provided a tentative indication of an interaction between trial type and condition, with the benefit of intermixed presentation being present for performance on different trials, but not on same trials.

Shipped coded 'failed' based on the pooled master table's binary 'Replicate (R) = no' indicator for the omnibus main effect of training condition across both same and different trials (F(1, 47) = 0.87, p = .335). However, in the individual primary replication report, the replication author explicitly concludes in the Discussion that 'We performed a close replication of Experiment 2 by Mitchell and colleagues (2008) and partially replicated their results,' finding the main effect of trial type (F(1, 47) = 181.95, p < .001) and a statistically significant intermixed-blocked advantage on the theoretically critical different trials (t(47) = 2.15, p = 0.037, dav = 0.43, with overlapping 95% CIs relative to the original effect), but no effect on same trials (t(47) = 0.33, p = 0.743) and no omnibus main effect across trial types. evidence.quote: This pattern of findings was replicated in the present study. In agreement with previous findings (Jones & Macken, 1995; Larsen et al., 2000; LeCompte & Shaibe, 1997; Marsh et al., 2008) showing that between-stream phonological similarity does not affect serial recall, between-stream phonological similarity had no effect on performance in the serial recall task, but free recall was more disrupted by phonologically similar distractors in comparison to phonologically dissimilar distractors. However, in contrast to the original study, the critical interaction between instruction type (free recall, serial recall) and sound condition (quiet, phonologically dissimilar, phonologically similar) was not significant. A supplementary analysis confirmed Marsh et al.’s finding that between-stream phonological similarity leads to intrusions errors in free recall. In the present study, phonologically similar speech led to more related-item intrusions in serial recall, too, suggesting that serial recall performance is not completely immune to the effects of between-stream phonological similarity (see Eagan & Chein, 2012, for a similar finding).
evidence.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/sqcwk/, Raoul Bell), Discussion, chunks 528-529 (lines 533-534)

Shipped coded 'failed' based on the pooled master table's binary 'Replicate (R) = no' entry for the 2x3 omnibus interaction (F(2, 232) = 1.63, p = .20). However, in the primary replication report's Results and Discussion, the replication author explicitly concludes that key findings of the original study were replicated—specifically, phonologically similar distractors significantly disrupted free recall compared to dissimilar distractors (t(58) = 4.42, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .25) while having no significant effect on serial recall performance (t(58) = 1.35, p = .18), and the supplementary analysis confirmed the original interaction showing phonological similarity intrusion errors in free recall (F(2, 116) = 15.28, p < .001)—whereas the omnibus 2x3 interaction between instruction type and sound condition was not significant and intrusions also occurred in serial recall. evidence.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt In the current study, we attempted to replicate the primary result of Study 5from Reynolds & Besner (2008), wherein there was no delay in responding when switching between stimulus categories while reading words and nonwords aloud. This effect was produced at two levels of analysis – participant-level, and stimulus item-level. In our replication with high power and a similar sample, we partially replicated the original results. We conducted both participant- level and item-level analyses and found that there was no significant evidence for a switch cost at the participant-level, but there was a switch cost when the data was analyzed at an item level. Lastly, there was an unexpected interaction between switch cost and stimulus type (i.e., word or nonword) when the data was analyzed at the participant level but not at the stimulus item level. Participants read words more slowly after a switch, but read nonwords at a similar speed regardless of whether there was a switch. In contrast to the reaction-time results, we fully replicated the error rate results from Study 5.
evidence.location: Primary Project Report: Replication of Contextual Effects on Reading Aloud: Evidence for Pathway Control by Reynolds & Besner (2008), Discussion / Summary of Replication Attempt (source_view.json lines 736-737)
evidence.reason: Prior Argon attempts timed out without producing output. Per Codebook Step 4 Rule 1, the authors' overall conclusion governs, and an explicitly partial verdict where some tested components succeed while others fail is coded 'mixed'. In the primary report for Reynolds & Besner (2008, Study 5), Simpson & Lai explicitly conclude that 'we partially replicated the original results': error rate analyses and the item-level interaction null (F(1, 92) = 1.95, p = .17) and participant-level switch-cost null (F(1, 19) = .03, p = .86) replicated, whereas an unexpected stimulus type x switch condition interaction emerged at the participant level (F(1, 19) = 4.77, p = .042) and a significant switch cost emerged at the item level (F(1, 92) = 5.62, p = .020). The shipped 'successful' coding relied solely on the single item-level interaction entry in the RPP spreadsheet rather than the primary report's overall partial verdict.

evidence.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The findings from the present study indicate a successful replication in terms of statistical significance. Specifically, a statistically significant omnibus Group x Problem Type interaction for RT as well as percentage of errors was found in our replication, replicating what was observed in the original study. However, the same pattern of response time means during the test phase were not found, indicating that different processes could have driven the two significant omnibus interactions. Commentary Despite the replication of the significant omnibus ANOVA from experiment three of the original study, there were differences in the pattern of results between the original study and the present replication.

Per Codebook Step 4, 'mixed' applies when 'some tested hypotheses, studies, measures, conditions or sites succeed while others fail; ... a multi-part prediction is only partly borne out; or the authors' overall verdict is explicitly qualified or partial.' In their Analysis Plan (line 540), Ricker & Saide pre-specified a two-part criterion: 'in order for the replication attempt to be considered successful, we expect both the interaction to be significant as well as the pattern of cell means to follow those reported in the original paper.' While the omnibus Group x Problem Type interactions for test RT (F(2, 68) = 41.603, p < .001) and error rate (F(2, 68) = 4.993, p = .009), same-operation savings, and the practice RT Block x Operation interaction replicated, the critical operation-change RT savings pattern failed to replicate (74 ms and 1 ms vs. original 330 ms and 302 ms; practice error interaction also non-significant, p = .109), leading the authors to conclude that 'The discrepancy between patterns of means, and potentially the effect driving the significant interaction, calls into question whether the present study should truly be considered a successful replication' (line 545).

expected_before.outcome_quote: We replicated three out of four expected contextual effects in the first attempt and all of them in the second attempt

evidence.quote: We replicated three out of four expected contextual effects in the first attempt and all of them in the second attempt. Though we ruled out some reasons (e.g. gender differences in samples) we were unable to determine why we did not get the hidden-zero effect in the first sample. More importantly, however, we found an interesting interaction of the hidden-zero effect with the addition of a common amount to both outcomes that replicated in both samples. Specifically the hidden-zero effect was stronger for smaller amounts but decreased as the amounts increased. Finally when we fit the extended tradeoff model to our data we found that it was most likely overfit to their data which was demonstrated both by the RMSD in our data using their estimates, the lack of stability of most of the parameters and by the larger error parameter in our estimations. Still we were able to estimate parameters that had a relatively low RMSD in the training sample and also had a low RMSD in the test sample suggesting that the model might indeed be tapping into parts of the decision process for these stimuli.

Addressing the retry feedback ('invalid replication outcome vocabulary' from using 'partially_successful' in attempt1) and the prior attempt2/blind coding of 'successful' based only on adjudicated_replication_code = 1 for a single test in raw_data.csv line 244: in the current snapshot (fields_2736b815e9f115a4_003.json) and blind coding (target 43), both shipped and blind have outcome = 'successful'. However, the codebook requires evaluating the full primary report for the original paper rather than a single extracted sub-test, and maps partial replication across tested findings/samples to the codebook vocabulary value 'mixed' (not 'partially_successful' or 'successful'). In read2012.pdf (line 706), the confirmatory plan tested four behavioral contextual effects plus the extended tradeoff model fit: (1) in Batch 1, 3 of 4 contextual effects replicated while the hidden-zero main effect failed (F(1, 296) = 1.899, p = 0.169, partial eta^2 = 0.006 vs. original F(1, 275) = 41.07, p < 0.005, partial eta^2 = 0.13); (2) in Batch 2, all 4 effects reached significance, though the hidden-zero effect was much smaller (F(1, 290) = 6.015, p = 0.015, partial eta^2 = 0.02) and qualified by an interaction with A0:2 (F(2, 580) = 9.092, p < 0.001); and (3) in the confirmatory tradeoff model fit, the original parameter estimates overfit (RMSD = 0.237 and 0.230, and large-difference spreading preference converged to zero), whereas re-estimated parameters achieved low RMSD (0.068 and 0.054) and preserved stability for key parameters q and kappa (matching the instructor rating of 0.75 in raw_data.csv line 244). evidence.rationale: The November 22, 2020 completed report by Hannah E. Marshall is the nook2017 project for the 2020–2021 cohort, not the October 11 proposal mistaken for a completed result. It names Study 1 and both focal findings; its actual N=56 and the exact Welch t=3.5641, df=1101.9 match the collection CSV. The author explicitly concludes that this is a failed replication attempt as a whole, after acknowledging partial replication of the distancing contrast, an opposite-direction distancing/regulation association, and exploratory agreement on reported affect. Under codebook outcome rule 1 this unqualified overall failed verdict governs; the smaller effect alone is not the reason for failure. The collection's final 0.75 score (instructor 0.75, report coder 0.5) is real contrary evidence and is not erased or replaced with a student numerical endpoint. The complete collection main text defines it as an ordinal subjective score with disagreements resolved by discussion, but supplies neither a categorical mixed verdict nor the project-specific rationale for 0.75. Thus it cannot automatically override or be equated with the primary report's explicit categorical verdict. The collection's single selected statistic covers only the agreeing distancing comparison, and the flagged degrees-of-freedom discrepancy is directly visible in the report; neither settles the broader outcome. The existing codebook supplies the categorical decision, without asserting that the ordinal score is wrong or that its provenance has been explained. The previous unknown depended on the report's absence, now resolved. Against shipped mixed, failed is a supported correction. No author verdict declares this attempt incapable of adjudication, so limitations do not make it uninformative.

evidence.rationale: Approve successful narrowly for agreement with Camerer (2018)'s Shah Study 1 finding, under codebook Step 3 rule 2 and its explicit original-null rule. The chain target remains Camerer, not Shah. The full original article and relevant SM now establish what that target found: Shah Study 1 failed in Camerer, with pooled r = −0.015, p = 0.710, N = 619 (SM Table 4), and the article treats the eight statistical failures as the eight default-Bayes-factor results supporting the null. Table 4 places Shah in that set; the original author's own failed Study 1 replication is explicitly described as consistent with/confirming Camerer's finding. This is substantive original-null evidence beyond a pair of nonsignificant p values. The current report retests the same poor-versus-rich Dots-Mixed comparison using Camerer's exact materials and reports a near-zero nonsignificant result, F(1,666) = .99, p = .319; its own discussion characterizes minimal cognitive influence. Thus both implicit-comparison tests pass: the original finding is established and the corresponding current result is identifiable. The current explicit failure verdict names Shah's positive finding; it is not an overall failure verdict against Camerer's null finding. The stated difference in sample-mean direction is retained, but neither report establishes a reverse substantive effect: Camerer's own signed estimate is near zero and its inferential interpretation supports absence of the positive scarcity effect. That sample-sign contrast is not a second tested finding that disagrees with Camerer's substantive conclusion, so it does not require mixed. Current authors decline to accept an exact null; this limits evidentiary strength and prevents an equivalence claim, but does not erase their directly corresponding result under the codebook. No overall Camerer-specific verdict overrides this implicit comparison. Approval concerns this one assigned comparison only, with no original-identity, type, removal, other-target or canonical change.

The current direct retest supplies the corresponding near-zero result; rule 2 permits an implicit comparison without a literal Camerer-success sentence.

Camerer does not present that tiny negative estimate as an established reverse effect; its substantive finding is failure of the positive effect with null support. Current authors do not establish a reverse effect relative to Camerer either. No second substantive finding disagrees.

proofs.quote: We observed that low-wealth subjects given fewer chances to win in repeated “Wheel of Fortune” type word puzzle games, performed worse on the Dots-Mixed attention task (M = 41.56, SD = 16.79) than high-wealth individuals (M = 42.82, SD = 15.87), however, this result was not statistically significant (F(1,666) = .99, p=.319). This result did not replicate the findings from Study 1 of Shah et al. (2012), but the means were not in the opposite direction of their results as seen in Camerer et al. (2018).

Although this project has neither the goal nor the capacity to “accept the null” hypothesis for any of these tests, the replications of these 20 studies indicate that within this set, scarcity primes have a minimal influence on cognitive ability, product attitudes, or well being.
Although most of our replications did not approach statistical significance, those that did (4, 16–18) shared some common features.
Camerer et al. (2018) replication of study 1 from “Some Consequences of Having Too Little” by Shah, Mullainathan, and Shafir (2012)
They also failed to replicate study 1 in their paper, consistent with our findings.
But importantly they also failed to replicate study 1 confirming our findings for that study.
† Replicated; significant effect (p < 0.05) in the same direction as in original study. ‡ Statistical power to detect 50% of the original effect size r. § Relative standardized effect size.
The default Bayes factor is below 1 for 8 (38.1%) studies, providing evidence in support of the null hypothesis; this evidence is strong to extreme for 4 (19.0%) studies.
A default Bayes factor48 above 1 favours the hypothesis of an effect in the direction of the original paper and a default Bayes factor below 1 favours the null hypothesis (H0) of no effect.

Bayesian Analysis. We computed the one-sided default Bayes factors for the replications31, as the hypotheses tested in the replications are clearly one-sided. Hence we obtain the strength of evidence in favor of the hypothesis that stipulates an effect in the direction of the original experiment (where a default prior is assigned to the size of the effect, that is, a folded Cauchy distribution with scale 0.707) versus the null hypothesis that stipulates the effect to be absent.

It resolves coder disagreements by discussion, but supplies no categorical translation of intermediate scores. The newly available report supplies an explicit overall author verdict under codebook rule 1; the ordinal fraction by itself supplies neither a conflicting categorical verdict nor a categorical veto. expected_before.outcome_quote: Our findings challenge the notion of consistent bias, as listeners did not uniformly perceive L1 Brazilian Portuguese speakers as more competent and comprehensible than L1 Spanish speakers, and, in fact, generally preferred treatment provided by L1 Spanish speakers.

evidence.quote:
Collectively, our findings underscore the complicated nature of accent bias, revealing complexities that surpass the insights from the initial study. For instance, Teló et al. (2022) identified speaker L1 as a significant predictor across all models, signifying that listeners generally perceived L1 English speakers as more competent and comprehensible than L2 English speakers, and that listeners generally wished to be treated as presented in scripts recorded by L1 versus L2 speakers. Here, this significance was not replicated across the models examining competence and comprehensibility, suggesting that the weight tied to speaker L1 alone was diminished, resulting in listeners not uniformly perceiving L1 BP speakers as more competent and comprehensible Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/applij/advance-article/doi/10.1093/applin/amae042/7712341 by University of Chicago D'Angelo Law Library user on 13 July 2024 C. Teló, R. Silveira, A. F. B. Marcelino, and M. G. O'Brien | 13
than L2 BP speakers. This difference across the studies is potentially related to the target languages, which in our study were Romance languages, likely contributing to mutual intelligibility. Furthermore, it may reflect the power differential between L1 BP and L1 Spanish speakers in Brazil, which is presumably different from the power imbalance observed between L1 English and L1 Tagalog speakers in Canada (Pennycook, 2010;Liddicoat, 2016). Additionally, in our treatment preference model, a divergence from the outcomes of the initial study surfaced: Listeners generally indicated a preference for treatment aligned with recordings from L2 BP speakers (see detailed discussion below). This unexpected twist implies that L1 background may interact with other (contextual, vocal) cues in unforeseen ways. Beyond L1 per se, the listeners in the current replication exhibited a heightened effect of speakers' accentedness; in fact, this was the only variable that consistently emerged as significant across all models. Speakers who were rated as having weaker accents were judged as more competent and comprehensible compared to those who were rated as having stronger accents. This trend also extended to treatment preference ratings, where speakers with less prominent accents were favored. While this finding clearly implies a gradient (rather than categorical) influence of accent on evaluations (Ryan et al. 1977), it likely stems from the Spanish speakers' pronunciation posing little or virtually no difficulty of understanding to L1 BP-speaking listeners, given the degree of similarity between the phonological inventories of the two languages. It is possible that, because the L2 BP speakers were rated as comprehensible as the L1 BP speakers, listeners paid greater attention to (and were more critical of) speakers' accentedness, once it was the only linguistic dimension that set L1 and L2 speakers apart. Regardless, listeners favoring weaker accents over stronger accents (both in the initial study and here) is supported by previous research showing that customers prefer to interact with professionals with weaker accents (Tsunemoto et al. 2023). Additionally, it might suggest that listeners perceive more 'nativelike' accents (i.e. more phonetic-phonologically similar to the target language) as indicative of better communication proficiency (Derwing and Munro 2009). In turn, listeners may have upgraded these speakers assuming that they were professionals who possess valuable workplace characteristics, such as dynamism, sense of initiative, and leadership skills (Beaulieu et al. 2022). On a theoretical level, we may assume that the linguistic similarity between BP and Spanish yields high levels of speaker comprehensibility, which, according to the processing fluency account of accent discrimination (Dragojevic and Giles 2016), should result in lower levels of accent discrimination overall in the present study when compared to the initial study. While our results may, indeed, demonstrate this to a certain extent, it is noteworthy that even though the listeners perceived the L1 and the L2 speakers comparably comprehensible, they showed clear accent-based biases. This provides support for categorization and stereotyping accounts of accent discrimination (e.g., Ryan 1983).

evidence.quote:
Although our results do not cast any doubt on the robustness of the red-anger effect in

within-subjects designs, we did not observe the red-anger effect at first impression, which

evidence.reason: The authors replicate the original red-anger effect in within-subjects designs across both Study 1 (close replication) and Study 2 (conceptual replication), while demonstrating via suspicion checks and a between-subjects absence-of-demand condition that the effect vanishes when demand characteristics are eliminated. Because the paper's central message and overall conclusion are that the replicated effect is an artifact of demand characteristics in the original within-subjects method, the special verdict 'statistically successful but flawed' applies.

evidence.quote: When analysing the entire clinical group, their self-estimated BMI closely matched their actual BMI, evidenced by a regression slope close to one (see Fig 2), suggesting a relatively accurate perception of own body size across the actual BMI range. However, excluding the participants with a history of bulimia nervosa and repeating the analysis, yielded results more consistent with Cornelissen et al. [17,18], as illustrated in Fig 3. Specifically, the regression slope of estimated BMI on actual BMI had a slope > 1, with accurate estimation at low actual BMI, and systematically increasing overestimation as actual BMI increased. How should we reconcile these differences in the results? We argue that our most important finding is that both multivariate analyses revealed a statistically significant interaction between participant group and actual BMI, irrespective of the inclusion or exclusion of participants with a history of bulimia nervosa.

(2015) [17] (as well as [18], which shares the identical comparisons): the authors confirm replication of the actual BMI x group interaction (line 140), normal contraction bias in controls, and the independent psychological (PSYCH) effect (line 132), which are individual tested effects rather than an overall replication verdict. evidence.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The main aim of this study was to test whether an interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility would predict the mean proportion of missed PM cues, in a three-way mixed ANOVA including also ongoing task as a between-subjects factor. This result was partially replicated: the interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility was strongly significant, however it was qualified by a three-way interaction with ongoing task, revealing that the effect was present only for participants in the location task condition but not for participants in the direction task condition. Also several, but not all, secondary results were successfully replicated and in addition some effects that were not present in the original paper resulted significant in this study (this might be partly due to the bigger sample size, and henceforth greater power, of this study, N=95, compared to the original study, N=40). evidence.reason: In the primary replication report for Goschke & Dreisbach (2008, Psychological Science, 19, 25-32, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02042.x), the confirmatory 2 x 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA yielded a significant two-way interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility (F(1, 93) = 18.94, p < .001), but in that same confirmatory model the effect was qualified by a significant three-way interaction with ongoing task (F(1, 93) = 12.22, p < .001), showing that the focal two-way interaction held only in the location task condition (F(1, 48) = 37.19, p < .001) and not in the direction task condition (F(1, 45) = .31, p = .582). In both the Summary of Replication Attempt and Commentary, the replicating authors explicitly conclude that 'This result was partially replicated,' that 'several, but not all, secondary results were successfully replicated,' and that 'the results are inconclusive concerning the underlying theoretical explanation.' Shipped coding ('successful') relied on the binary summary sheet column for the isolated 2-way F-test (and quoted the original effect description rather than an outcome verdict). Under the codebook rules—where confirmation of one test is not confused with the overall verdict and findings explicitly described by the authors as 'partially replicated' because they hold only in a subset of conditions are coded as 'mixed'—blind coding ('mixed') is right.

evidence.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The central goal of the current study was to investigate the replicability of the effects reported in Experiment 5 of Demany et al. (2008). We were able to replicate the significant main effect of ISI which showed that performance worsened as the interval between a chord and tone increased. Next, we also replicated the non-significant main effect of N, showing that N did not significantly affect performance. Finally, in contrast with the original study, we found that the effect of ISI on performance did not differ between chords with small or large N. Given that these data follow two of the three trends found by Demany et al. (2008), the current study qualifies as a partial replication. Commentary While this study qualifies only as a partial replication, we believe it is important to point out that the significant ISI x N interaction found in Experiment 5 was not anticipated given the prior trends and conclusions from Experiments 1, 2, and 4. Indeed, it was reported to only have occurred due to "unexpectedly high d' when N was equal to 1 and the ISI was 0 ms". Importantly, the central finding of Experiment 5 was replicated. Therefore, we believe our data to be mostly in line with the effects found by Demany et al. (2008).
evidence.location: PRIMARY PROJECT REPORT 59 (https://osf.io/download/wx74s/), Discussion - Summary of Replication Attempt and Commentary, source_view.json lines 679-680 (chunk_index 676-677)
evidence.reason: In Primary Project Report 59 (Demany, Trost, Serman, & Semal, 2008, Experiment 5), the Analysis Plan pre-specified three criteria for a successful replication: a significant main effect of ISI, a non-significant main effect of N, and a significant N x ISI interaction. While the project master table (Study Num 139) records Replicate (R) = yes for the single key main effect of ISI (F(3, 12) = 13.06, p < .001) and the Commentary notes that the central finding was replicated, the confirmatory ANOVA replicated two of the three pre-specified effects (significant main effect of ISI and non-significant main effect of N) but failed to replicate the significant N x ISI interaction (p > .05), leading the authors to explicitly conclude in both the Summary of Replication Attempt and Commentary that 'the current study qualifies as a partial replication' / 'qualifies only as a partial replication'. Under the codebook, an explicit author verdict of partial replication where some focal tested effects replicate and another does not maps to mixed.

expected_before.outcome_quote: Coded as successfully replicated: Replicate = 1 (the project's binary success indicator combining significance and direction).

evidence.quote: In the original study by Alvarez and Oliva (2008, Exp.3), the hypothesis was supported that distractor centroids can be localized better than chance, but single distractors cannot. This finding shows that there is an ability to process visual features outside the focus of attention. In this replication we found that both multiple and single distractors can be localized better than chance. That means we could replicate the result for centroid localization, but not for single distractor localization.
evidence.location: Primary Report 36 (Alvarez & Oliva, 2008 replication report), Discussion - Summary of Replication Attempt (view lines 470-471, source char offset 840442)
evidence.reason: Prior Argon attempts timed out on the full 100-study bundle without returning decisions. In the individual primary replication report for Alvarez and Oliva (2008, Experiment 3), the authors test both components of the original finding and explicitly conclude that they replicated the centroid-localization effect (distractor centroids localized better than chance) and manipulation check, but failed to replicate the single-distractor finding (single distractors were also localized better than chance, contradicting the original null result), stating that the results were only partially replicated. The shipped 'successful' value relied solely on the aggregate dataset's single-test binary indicator rather than the primary report's mixed findings.

expected_before.outcome_quote: An online replication (Study 1, N = 214) provided evidence that, when participants exerted low (yet still acceptable) levels of response effort to the experimental material, cleanliness priming led to more lenient moral judgments than neutral priming.

evidence.quote: Unlike Study 1 that measured naturally occurring response effort, Study 2 manipulated response effort on the sentence unscrambling task. Support for the cleanliness hypothesis was found among participants instructed to work through the sentence unscrambling task as quickly as possible. In contrast, when participants were instructed to work on the sentence unscrambling task attentively, no support was found for the hypothesized effect of the cleanliness priming.
evidence.reason: Across both Study 1 and Study 2, the overall unmoderated cleanliness priming effect was non-significant, with the original effect replicating only among low-effort participants and failing to hold among high-effort participants, establishing response effort as a boundary condition and yielding a mixed outcome.

evidence.quote: We failed to replicate Austerweil & Griffith’s (2011) key result—that changing the prior probability of underlying rules changed how likely people were to test certain hypotheses—using a chi-squared test. It is worth noting that the results of our chi-squared test were likely inaccurate because several cells had a very small number of responses. In order to circumvent this bias, we instead analyzed the data using a mixed-effect logistic regression. Using this analysis, we indeed found that training condition predicted how often participants tested each class of rule.
evidence.location: PRIMARY PROJECT REPORT: austerweil2011.pdf, Discussion / Summary of Replication Attempt (line 412)
evidence.reason: The replication (N = 50, compared with original N = 29) failed to replicate the key effect using the planned chi-squared test (p = 0.28, or p = 0.11 excluding 'other' responses) but replicated the effect using a mixed-effect logistic regression (p < 0.001), yielding an adjudicated score of 0.75. Because the finding failed under the original analysis and succeeded under the alternative model, the outcome is mixed rather than uninformative.

evidence.quote: I was able to fully replicate the significance of this difference, but the finding is not as robust as the original, as reflected in the weaker evidence shown in the p values and F values. The figure I produced from the replication also looks qualitatively similar to the original, but the original did not provide error bars or discuss standard error of the mean or confidence intervals, so I’m not entirely sure how similar the figures are in terms of data variability. Commentary Interestingly, even though I was able to replicate the original study’s finding regarding affect, my exploratory analysis did not find that attitude was more negative toward Asian Americans when realistic threat was induced. My replication indicates that inducing realistic threat influences emotion, but not attitudes, towards Asian Americans.
evidence.location: OSF Primary Source: maddux2008.html, Discussion -> Summary of Replication Attempt & Commentary (texts/2736b815e9f115a4.txt, line 636); see also raw_data.csv line 234
evidence.reason: In maddux2008.html (replicating Maddux, Galinsky, Cuddy, & Polifroni, 2008, Study 3, DOI 10.1177/0146167207309195; paired_target_index 35), the original Study 3 demonstrated that realistic threat caused both negative attitude (7-point bipolar scale, the "main attitude measure") and negative affect (0-100 feeling thermometer) toward Asian Americans. The replication author replicated the significant difference on the affect thermometer (F(1, 76) = 4.779, p = .032, eta2 = .060), but also administered and tested the original Study 3 attitude scale (finding no significant difference, F(1, 76) = 1.564, p = .215, eta2 = .020) and explicitly contrasted this non-replication with the original Study 3 finding in the Discussion Commentary: "even though I was able to replicate the original study’s finding regarding affect, my exploratory analysis did not find that attitude was more negative toward Asian Americans when realistic threat was induced. My replication indicates that inducing realistic threat influences emotion, but not attitudes, towards Asian Americans." Under Codebook Rule 1 and Rule 2, confirming one focal effect ("I was able to fully replicate the significance of this difference") is one comparison rather than an overall verdict on the replication as a whole, and a tested original finding that the report itself explicitly contrasts with the original cannot be left out of the verdict even if labeled exploratory relative to the single focal class assignment test. Furthermore, the full primary report overrides the single-test 1/1 summary row in raw_data.csv. Thus both shipped and blind "successful" codings are wrong, and the corrected value is "mixed".

evidence.quote:
That is, for both the experimental condition that
produced the lowest inclusion of women (i.e., masculine
generics) and the highest inclusion of women (capital-I),
the number of women listed by participants in the present
study and by participants two decades ago did not differ statistically. Although not a true experimental test, this convergence in absolute numbers indicates that the changes
regarding the visibility and increased power of women in
society did not lead to an overall increased cognitive accessibility of women. Only for masculine-feminine word pairs,
our results differed from the original study. In our replication, significantly more women were listed in this condition
than in the masculine generics condition, whereas this contrast was not significant in the original study.
evidence.reason: Evaluating the hierarchy of statements across the full source shows that the outcome is mixed rather than successful. First, the pairwise contrast between masculine-feminine word pairs and masculine generics is a core tested finding of the original 3x2 design that the authors explicitly highlighted in the Introduction (p. 2, lines 108-125) and powered their study to test (p. 5, lines 420-422). Second, in Results (p. 8, lines 897-902), the statement 'Taken together, our results replicate those found by Stahlberg et al. (2001)' is immediately scoped by 'In particular, (1)... (2)... (3)... (4)...' to the four ANOVA-level patterns (the omnibus effect of linguistic expression, the relative ordering where capital-I exceeds word pairs, the main effect of participant gender, and the null interaction); it does not cover the simple contrast of word pairs versus masculine generics, and the immediately following paragraph (lines 903-915) shows that the word-pair condition mean differed significantly from the original study. Third, when synthesizing the replication as a whole in the opening paragraph of the Discussion (pp. 9-10, lines 1111-1154), the authors themselves qualify the convergence as holding for the pattern of main effects and for 2 of the 3 original conditions (masculine generics and capital-I), while explicitly marking the third condition as a deviation: 'Only for masculine-feminine word pairs, our results differed from the original study. In our replication, significantly more women were listed in this condition than in the masculine generics condition, whereas this contrast was not significant in the original study.' Under the codebook, finding an effect where the original found none is a disagreement (not merely a stronger effect size), and when a paper confirms the focal effect it set out to test while explicitly marking another tested finding as differing from the original in its own words, the summary of focal/main effects does not override the stated contrast and the outcome must be coded as mixed.

evidence.rationale: Cristina Ceballos's December 13, 2019 completed Study 1 report matches rottman2019 in the 2019–2020 cohort: 162 recruited minus 5 excluded yields the reported 157, with exact dosage-difference means/SDs 11.5(17.9) for harm and 4.48(17.3) for purity, matching the collection record and original 14.605(20.395)/4.185(16.060). Target/cohort/sample/statistic and the registered RPubs pointer establish binding. The discussion explicitly states 'Overall, my replication seems to have been successful', covering the replication as a whole, not just an isolated test. Under codebook rule 1 this supports successful. Contrary results are substantive: the report flags that the domain-by-dosage interaction is not significant, prints -6.8322, SE=9.0497, t=-.755 with a convergence warning, and its reduced model also lacks the original clear dosage effect. The author nevertheless judges overall success from the corresponding dosage-sensitivity pattern. No p-value is computed and the sign/wording discrepancy is not repaired. Under the hierarchy these issues do not justify replacing the whole-attempt verdict with our own mixed/failed judgment. The instructor/report/final scores .5/.75/.5, including the adjudicated .5, are retained as a conflicting ordinal appraisal; the SI p-original .085 is also retained, not treated as categorical. The complete collection main report says independent subjective ratings were reconciled by discussion; these are broader ordinal assessments rather than just the selected statistic. The complete official five-page supplement adds heterogeneity/model/sensitivity results and a forest plot, with no project-specific categorical conversion key or alternative categorical overall verdict. Its statement that some statistical mismatches retained reliable holistic scores does not identify a categorical verdict for this project. The collection scores are preserved as contrary or qualifying evidence, without asserting that they are erroneous. Neither .5 nor .75 is converted automatically to mixed. The existing codebook's explicit overall-author-verdict hierarchy supplies the categorical decision from the recovered completed primary report. The previously missing primary narrative is now fully read; the earlier evidence-limit objection no longer applies. The shared issue comment records a curator's intermediate-score mapping, not a categorical verdict printed in the collection or an author quotation. Shipped boilerplate remains a provenance problem outside the assigned outcome field. Against shipped mixed, successful is correction_supported; the underlying ratings themselves are not being changed. The source does not characterize the attempt as uninformative; original-data work in the methods supplies power planning, not an additional outcome assigned here.

The new complete Study 2 narrative matches the collection by the same founding-penalty question, t=-0.80127 with df=155.59 and final N=188 (239 responses minus 51 exclusions). It explicitly considers the failed unadjusted test, then interprets the gender interaction model as recovering the primary finding and gives an overall verdict favouring replication. evidence.quote:
Evidence that affective factors (e.g. anxiety, depression, affect) are significantly related to individual differences in emotion recognition is mixed. Palermo et al. (Palermo et al. 2018 J. Exp. Psychol. Hum. Percept. Perform.
44, 503–517) reported that individuals who scored lower in anxiety performed significantly better on two measures of facial-expression recognition (emotion-matching and emotion-labelling tasks), but not a third measure (the multimodal emotion recognition test). By contrast, facial-expression recognition was not significantly correlated with measures of depression, positive or negative affect, empathy, or autistic-like traits. Because the range of affective factors considered in this study and its use of multiple expression-recognition tasks mean that it is a relatively comprehensive investigation of the role of affective factors in facial expression recognition, we carried out a direct replication.
evidence.location: Primary abstract and full Introduction/Methods/Discussion; all shipped rows951/2156 checked
evidence.reason: Full primary article explicitly carries out the Palermo2018 facial-expression/anxiety retest, already correctly represented in row951 (DOI10.1037/xhp0000463). Row2156 instead supplies Berggren/Eimer visual-search paper10.1037/xhp0000541 while quoting the same Palermo finding. Entire primary retest/design/reference chain selects Palermo; substituting Palermo into2156 would duplicate951. Retain951, remove2156; no extra missing reference or second outcome transfer. Independent parent source inspection, not the initial expert replacement proposal.

expected_before.outcome_quote: In Study 1, which was a conceptual replication with real luxury brands, we did not observe an effect of luxury products on partner devotion but found that women assumed that male partners contribute financial resources to women’s luxury possessions. In Study 2, which was a direct replication with designer products, we observed a small-sized effect in the opposite direction, such that perceived partner devotion increased when women used nondesigner products.

evidence.quote:
We present two preregistered replications of the paper by Wang and Griskevicius
(2014), which reported that women flaunt luxury products to signal their partners’
devotion, thereby guarding their relationships from rivals. In Study 1, which was a
conceptual replication with real luxury brands, we did not observe an effect of
luxury products on partner devotion but found that women assumed male partners
contribute financial resources to women’s luxury possessions. In Study 2, which
was a direct replication with designer products, we observed a small-sized effect in
the opposite direction, such that perceived partner devotion increased when women
used nondesigner products. Similar to Study 1, perceived partner contribution to
possessions was higher for designer products.
evidence.reason: The authors explicitly frame both perceived partner devotion (H1) and assumed partner financial contribution (H2) as the two main postulations and hypotheses of Wang and Griskevicius (2014) tested across both replication studies (distinct from the manipulation check and the Study 1 benevolent-sexism extension). Because H1 failed to replicate (and reversed in Study 2) while H2 was consistently supported across both studies, and no overall verdict overrides this contrast, the outcome is mixed.

Specifically, we found support for partition dependence in scenarios from Study 1a Items 1 and 2, Study 1b and Study 3, with weaker effects, yet with no consistent support for Study 1a Item 3 and Study 4. evidence.quote:
Nevertheless, what remains difficult to understand is why the targeted
COMT
-X-disorganization interaction only predicted change over time in the original Norwegian research and not levels of child behavior at either 4 or 6 years. Here, though, we found in our primary analyses that when disorganization was (a) measured categorically rather than continuously, (b) using the gold-standard Strange Situation rather than a story-stem completion task, and (c) at 15 months rather than at 4 years of age, that levels of kindergarten social behavior reported (only) by mothers could be accounted for by considering the moderation by
COMT
of attachment disorganization. Quite conceivably, these measurement and design differences across studies are responsible for the differences in findings across the two studies.
In any event, reasonably consistent support for the Norwegian hypothesis emerged in both inquiries as to why some children with disorganized attachment histories behave in seemingly controlling-caregiving and others in controlling-punitive ways. Especially notable, perhaps, is that in both studies the genetically-related divergent patterns of functioning are restricted to maternal reports of child behavior, thereby underscoring the relationship-specificity of disorganized attachment, at least when examined from the perspective of a gene -X-disorganization interaction.
evidence.reason: Both the shipped row and blind coding record 'successful' by treating the authors' statements of support for 'the Norwegian hypothesis' as an unqualified Rule 1 whole-original replication verdict. However, in both the Introduction and the primary/sensitivity Discussion, Li et al. (2016) explicitly distinguish Hygen et al.'s (2014) initial theoretical hypothesis from Hygen et al.'s actual empirical findings: in Hygen et al. (2014), the COMT x attachment disorganization interaction predicted only change in social behavior from age 4 to 6 and did not predict levels of child behavior at age 4 or 6, whereas Li et al. (2016) tested and found the COMT x disorganization interaction for levels of social functioning (at kindergarten and Grade 6), explicitly acknowledging 'the differences in findings across the two studies' (alongside sensitivity analyses indicating a linear 3-level gene effect rather than Hygen et al.'s nonlinear 2-level pattern). Because agreement with an original hypothesis does not override the authors' explicit contrast between the original change-only/null-levels finding and the present levels finding, aggregating the confirmed and contrasting original-specific empirical comparisons yields 'mixed'.

evidence.quote: Here we reexamine Moran et al.’s data using more fine-grained analytic strategies. First, for Research Question 1 (the main models testing verb restrictiveness and talker accent on predictive sentence processing), the primary source states both Porretta et al.'s original finding and the corresponding replication result, and explicitly concludes that the replication succeeded across both GLMM and GAMM analyses ('We observed nearly identical time course of predictive processing (Figure 11) in which restricted sentences resulted in earlier looks to the target object than nonrestrictive sentences. Further, this effect is partially reduced in accented speech in a similar manner to Porretta et al. (2020)', Section 4.3, lines 3761-3769; 'Our main models show that predictive sentence processing is modulated by restrictive and non-restrictive verb type in line with Porretta et al. (2020) and that accented speech impedes predictive processing but does not preclude it', Section 5.1, lines 3844-3854). Second, for Research Question 2 (the accent-experience models), the primary source lists Porretta et al.'s second research question ('2) To what extent does accent experience modulate prediction in accented speech?', Section 3.1, lines 834-837) and reports Porretta et al.'s sample mean/SD of Chinese accent exposure (1.78, SD = 0.82, Section 3.2.3, lines 1076-1081), but never states what Porretta et al.'s accent-experience analysis actually found. Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 2a ('Two tests before you code from an implicit comparison, and both must pass: (a) the evidence states what THE ORIGINAL THIS OUTCOME IS ABOUT found. You cannot compare against a finding the evidence never states, however positive this paper's own results sound'), a research question is not an original finding, so the accent-experience null cannot establish a failed comparison against Porretta et al. (2020). Moreover, the authors themselves explicitly restrict direct replication comparison to RQ1 in Section 3.1 ('A direct comparison can be made between our study and Porretta et al. (2020) for research question one... For research question two, our interpretation will be limited given our random sample of Prolific participants (i.e., we are not controlling experience with Chinese-accented English)', lines 839-847) and explicitly declare their accent models uninformative/inconclusive due to lower sample exposure, insufficient statistical power (49 analyzed vs. ~90 needed), and slider measurement error in Section 5.1 ('Our results are, therefore, inconclusive with respect to the accent models', p. 41, lines 3914-3916). Because the sole established comparison with Porretta et al. (2020) succeeded and the secondary accent-model test is both missing the original finding in the text and declared inconclusive by the authors, the outcome is 'successful'.

expected_before.outcome_quote: Our overall results were consistent with Crosby et al.’s original report. We found that, on hearing an offensive remark, subjects were significantly more likely to gaze toward a potentially offended person if that person could hear the offensive remark than if he could not. However, we did not find that subjects’ behavior in the task was affected by the protocol to which they had been assigned: The social-referencing effect did not differ significantly between subjects assigned to our new protocol and those assigned to the protocol that Jonas and Skorinko (2015) used in the RP:P. This raises the question of why the original finding was not replicated in Jonas and Skorinko’s study, but was replicated in ours, given that our protocol manipulation did not appear to affect subjects’ behavior. One answer, we propose, lies in the observation that the key effect size found in our replication was considerably smaller than that found in Crosby et al.’s original study.

The smaller effect and methodological cautions do not amount to an author verdict of an uninformative or statistically successful but flawed attempt. One original paper is targeted; no missing pair is inferred from protocol reuse. Publication DOI 10.1177/2515245919870737 is independently recorded in institutional/Crossref metadata, not claimed as printed in this manuscript. expected_before.outcome_quote: We found strong empirical support for the pattern that (1) innocent intentions induce more lenient wrongness judgements for accidentals, but weak empirical support for the pattern that (2) bad intentions induce harsher wrongness judgements for failed attempts, to a significantly larger extent for harm violations compared to purity violations. Intent plays a critical role for wrongness judgements of harm versus purity violations. Contrary to the original study, however, pattern (1) was not specific to moral judgements versus disgust ratings; and pattern (2) was not specific to moral judgements versus emotion ratings.

evidence.rationale: The newly supplied complete 99-page public preprint is directly linked to mutable public OSF project 2egqr by the saved node/folder/file metadata and identity receipt; no identity with the different qswe3/u59ab thesis is assumed. Having independently read all 166,079 characters of the main report and supplementary, I agree with the fresh sanitized proposal on the outcome, using it only as a proposal. The abstract explicitly states that the authors successfully replicated and extended Experiments 1A and 2 to 4 of Young and Saxe (2011). This is a genuine overall verdict about the named replication set, rather than confirmation of just one effect. Under codebook rule 1 that verdict governs the single original-paper outcome. The discussion also says all original significant effects were successfully replicated. The strongest alternative is mixed: results give partial support for adjusted hypotheses 2 and 3, and the discussion/conclusion explicitly contrast emotion and disgust specificity with the original. Those are real original-specific countercomparisons, not extension-only or irrelevant analyses, and would support mixed under rule 2 absent the overall verdict. Nevertheless the later synthesis describes strong and weak support and non-specificity without retracting the set-wide successful verdict or declaring the replication overall partial/mixed. Thus it qualifies the successful verdict rather than superseding it. Experiment 2's adjusted comparison is included by the abstract, even though the all-significant-effects summary alone would not settle its original null findings. Smaller effects and signal-inconsistent labels alone do not make mixed. Moral responsibility is an expressly separate extension and its support or contrast with Parkinson and Byrne does not decide this Young/Saxe outcome. The old cached text genuinely contains explicit randomized-data warnings and an unfinished Stage 2 discussion, so its cannot_be_determined judgment remains a valid source-bound prior opinion. Those warnings do not describe this new completed report, which states completed collection, supplies actual main results and a substantive discussion, and documents pre/post-exclusion results and a corrected emotion-rating coding deviation. Residual supplementary templates do not negate these results; authors do not give an uninformative or statistically-successful-but-flawed verdict. The old claim that no completed report linked to 2egqr is available is now superseded by this new evidence; no outcome is transferred from another record. Only row 2388 outcome is proposed for correction, from shipped mixed/current cannot_be_determined to successful.

contrary_evidence.resolution: A substantive partial replication comparison for adjusted hypothesis 2, retained; the explicit overall named-experiment verdict has priority.
A substantive partial replication comparison for adjusted hypothesis 3, retained; the explicit overall verdict has priority.

The conclusion is the strongest mixed argument and corresponds to the shipped quote. It summarizes supported patterns and specificity departures but never calls the replication as a whole partial/mixed or withdraws the abstract verdict.
This original-specific emotion contrast concerns the tested replication, not merely an extension. It qualifies rather than replaces the overall verdict.
This original-specific disgust contrast concerns the tested replication. It remains a real contrary comparison, governed by rule 1.

expected_before.outcome_quote: In this paper, we demonstrate that the neighborhood-level predictors of positive COVID-19 test counts in New York City modelled by DiMaggio et al. during the first wave of the pandemic remained associated with positive test counts in Phoenix, AZ. expected_before.outcome_quote: ABSTRACT. This study is a partial replication of L. Hu and P. M. Bentler's (1999) fit criteria work. The purpose of this study was twofold: (a) to determine whether cut-off values vary according to which model is the true population model for a dataset and (b) to identify which of 13 fit indexes behave optimally by retaining all of the correct models while simultaneously rejecting all of the misspecified models in a manner invariant across sample size and data distribution. The authors found that for most indexes the results do not vary depending on which model serves as the correct model. Furthermore, the search for an optimal cut-off value led to a new discovery about the nature of McDonald's measure of centrality and the root mean square error of approximation. Unlike all other indexes considered in this study, the cut-off value of both indexes actually decreases for incorrect models as sample size increases.

In Experiment 1 (Chapter 3, Section 3.10.1.1, pp. 89–90), Toomer replicates all four declarative claims for technical collocations, while his procedural priming finding in the reading-only condition after 9 exposures across two days is an explicit dose extension fulfilling Sonbul and Schmitt’s (p. 153) prediction rather than a replication failure. However, Experiment 2 (Chapter 4) is not solely an extension without original-finding comparison: alongside extending to lexical (V+N) versus grammatical (prep+N) collocations, its Research Questions 1–2 (p. 98) conceptually re-test the same exposure and typographic-enhancement claims, and Section 4.8.2 (pp. 140–141) explicitly benchmarks both against Sonbul and Schmitt (2013). expected_before.outcome_quote: We successfully replicated the basic congruency effect of the original study, that is, the interaction effect between direction of manual response and time reference when participants perform a sensicality judgment. In contrast to the original study, this congruency effect was not significantly modulated by the magnitude of time shift.

evidence.quote: Although the threefold interaction between Response location, Time shift direction, and Shift magnitude on RT was not signiﬁcant in our study, our results largely replicate those of Sell and Kaschak (2011).
evidence.reason: Under Rule 1 and the codebook's 'mixed' definition, a component-level contrast ('In contrast to the original study, this congruency effect was not significantly modulated by the magnitude of time shift') is outweighed when the authors state a genuine overall verdict speaking to the replication as a whole. In both the Abstract and Discussion, the authors do not merely assert confirmation of the focal two-way congruency effect before reporting a contrast; rather, after reviewing the non-significant by-participant three-way interaction alongside the significant by-item three-way interaction, the matching qualitative pattern in Figure 1, and the separate simple-interaction analyses showing a significant congruency effect for large but not small time shifts, they issue an explicit post-contrast synthesis covering 'our results' as a whole: 'Although the threefold interaction ... was not significant in our study, our results largely replicate those of Sell and Kaschak (2011). Therefore, the present replication enforces the conclusion of the original study...' (mirroring the Abstract's 'In sum, this replication reinforces the basic conclusion by Sell and Kaschak... especially when the time shift is large'). Here 'largely replicate' functions as an overall affirmative replication verdict that explicitly subordinates the single non-significant omnibus interaction rather than framing the replication outcome as mixed.

evidence.location: Section 7 Conclusion and Future Work, pp. 144-145 (chunk 56, chars 59162-60216; see also chunks 57-58 and Section 8, chunk 62)
evidence.reason: Because the study is a digital re-analysis of the same 11 Racine plays examined by Spitzer (1931 [1928]) before expanding to a comparative corpus, its study type is reproduction, requiring the two-part reproduction outcome schema rather than a single replication outcome string. Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, so exact computational reproduction of original numerical outputs was not checked. In the first phase re-analyzing the original 11 Racine plays via formal CQP queries in TXM on annotated texts, 24 of the roughly 50 stylistic patterns identified by Spitzer could be formally modeled (making the methodological transposition of the full 50-pattern catalog only partially feasible), and for those modeled patterns the analysis verified Spitzer's cited examples and showed that the dampening patterns are even more frequent in Racine's work than Spitzer showed (robust). The subsequent finding that these patterns occur at similar rates in contemporaries—making classical dampening a genre/period style rather than a unique authorial signature—relies on a newly introduced comparative corpus of 38 contemporary plays and does not negate the confirmation of the patterns' prevalence within Racine's plays.

Although Forsythe's (2022) original dataset and code were publicly archived on Zenodo, the replicators did not run the original dataset or code. Instead, they reconstructed the 1994-2014 CPS dataset from scratch via IPUMS-CPS using modified longitudinal matching criteria (stricter age/race tolerances yielding 16,208,583 regression observations vs. 16,948,516 in the original paper), IPUMS-harmonized education, industry, and occupation variables, zero-imputation for negative potential experience, and an unfiltered Table 6 sample. The authors report that their regressions replicate the original results very closely in sign, significance, and magnitude and attribute the minor numerical differences across tables to their alternative dataset construction procedure. Because the identical original dataset was never rerun and the reconstructed-sample analysis is a test of analytical robustness (which succeeded), computational reproducibility of the original numbers was not checked.

evidence.quote:
This is a replication of Mayshar et al. (2022) (henceforth MMP).1 The article posits
that the state (defined as societal hierarchy such as tax-levying elites) originated from
cultivation of appropriable cereal grains, contrary to the conventional theory that the
state originated from increased land productivity following the adoption of agriculture.
The article uses multiple datasets to demonstrate a causal effect of cereal cultivation on
hierarchy (Claim 1) without finding a similar effect for land productivity (Claim 2), and
that societies based on roots or tubers display levels of hierarchy similar to nonfarming
societies (Claim 3).

evidence.quote:
We have two main results. 1) Gaps between elite and mass decision-making are larger in studies
whose manipulations appear to have worked. Only a small number of the these 162 treatments
significantly affected masses (N=28) or elites (N=30). This low rate suggests the possibility that
almost all of these experiments failed to successfully manipulate either masses or elites. If so, we
may not be able to conclude that masses and elites respond similarly to experiments with confidence
until political scientists produce more experiments with actual treatment effects or with successful
manipulation checks in cases of null effects.
evidence.reason: The shipped quote reflects only the intermediate summary of the first two checks (study inclusion criteria and treatment pooling) halfway through Section 3.1. Across the full pre-registered robustness and heterogeneity re-analyses of Claim 1, the authors find that when restricting to studies with significant mass or elite treatment effects (successful manipulations), the rate of statistically significant mass-elite differences rises from 12% to 43%-63% after FDR adjustment (vs. 7% when neither is significant). In both the Abstract and the Conclusion, the authors explicitly judge that these re-analyses materially qualify Kertzer's central inference that masses and elites respond similarly to experiments, fitting 'robustness challenges'.
